#9643. Building on Nemotron 3.5 Parse: Open Data, Fine-Tuning, and Faster Inference

We recently released NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Parse, a compact document model that turns page images into structured data for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and agents.

Now we’re building on that release with synthetic training datasets, a fine-tuning recipe, and a DFlash2 speculator for faster inference. We’re also sharing how we trained Parse 3.5: first teaching document understanding through supervised fine-tuning, then using reinforcement learning to improve accuracy, consistency, and reliable completion.

Parse extracts content from pages of documents into reading order, assigns content classes such as headings, paragraphs, tables, and charts, and returns bounding boxes that locate the content. Tables and charts become structured records that can power downstream document processing applications.

Figure 1. Actual model output from a synthetic operations brief, showing the connection between the page and its structured representation.

This latest version of Parse significantly extends its ability to read charts and tables, especially in more difficult and ambiguous cases. For example, bar charts or other plots that do not have any marked numeric values. The model is able to infer values by looking at the axes and height of the bar to derive these. Tables can be especially tricky because the structure is so meaningful, a shifted row or column can totally change the interpretation and meaning. These advancements have been largely powered by synthetic data generation, rendering variations of charts and tables with known ground truth and then training our model to reverse this process.

We are open-sourcing three datasets used in the Parse 3.5 training:

Synthetic Charts V1 — 9.98M examples: rendered charts and structured annotations for learning categories, series, and numerical values.

Synthetic Tables V1 — 1M examples: rendered HTML tables with targets that preserve rows, columns, headers, and cell relationships.

OCR Synthetic Multilingual v2 — 7.9M examples: synthetic document pages with Parse-format targets across varied fonts and layouts, for multilingual OCR and structured page reading.

Each release includes images, annotations, generation documentation, and the training format. Use these pairs to fine-tune document models or create new variations for a target document type or language.

Figure 2. Parse recovers 18, 27, 39, and 54 from the chart geometry

We trained Parse 3.5 with two phases of training. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) spanning text, layout, tables, charts, and multilingual documents. Learning to predict structured targets established the general capability of reading a page and representing its contents.

We then continued with reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). Rewards check the quality of sampled extractions. For example, a chart extraction can earn a better reward for recovering the correct series and values, producing a usable structure, and finishing without repeatedly generating the same content.

A difficult page can have several valid representations. These checks give the model flexibility to find a correct answer without prescribing one exact token sequence, while discouraging looping and unfinished output.

Figure 3. A controlled comparison of SFT and GRPO with matched evaluation settings. These are development checkpoints, separate from the final released model. Loop counts use a repetition check. Methods.

The matched comparison shows the benefit: loop-flagged outputs fall from 126 to 29 pages—about 77% fewer—and outputs reaching the 9,000-token limit fall from 185 to 35. Overall score improves from 66.24 to 71.38, including +5.18 points in tables and +4.15 in charts.

A parser must generate substantial text and structure for every page. Alongside the training work, we optimized how Parse 3.5 processes images and decodes those outputs.

NaViT preprocessing adapts the input shape to the page. A visual adapter compresses the image sequence, and the text decoder consumes it as a prefix, replacing encoder–decoder cross-attention. Grouped-query attention with eight key/value heads (GQA-8) reduces the decoder’s attention-cache memory.

The built-in multi-token prediction (MTP) head supplies one-token lookahead. Our DFlash2 speculator goes further: a small draft model proposes up to 32 tokens ahead, and Parse verifies the proposals together. In the measured 32-token configuration, it averages about 14 accepted draft tokens, or roughly 15 output tokens of progress per verification step including the target token.

Figure 4. Native single-pass throughput on one H200, BF16, using the same 2,078 pages. Parse 2.0 uses one trial per point; Parse 3.5 shows three-trial medians. Arrows show the gain from Parse 3.5 base to DFlash2. Measurement details.

In the native single-pass benchmark on one H200 in BF16, DFlash2 increased throughput 7.62× at concurrency 1 and 1.52× at concurrency 512, compared with Parse 3.5 with speculative decoding disabled. At 512, Parse 3.5 reaches 13.48 pages/s without speculation and 20.44 pages/s with DFlash2, versus 2.98 for Parse 2.0. Those are 4.53× and 6.86× the Parse 2.0 throughput, respectively.

Fast parsing gives us room to revisit difficult regions. Start with a full-page prediction, then add focused reprocessing where the document needs it:

Single pass - Parse the full page once for text, layout, tables, and charts.

Double pass - use for dense tables and small chart details. Crop the table and chart regions found by the parser, re-parse them at higher detail, and merge the refinements into the page output.

Triple pass - Instead of only using the models full page parsing bounding boxes, use a second pass of the model in detection mode in order to get verification that all boxes have been accurately found and text has not been missed and re-extract any found charts or tables in a third pass

Figure 5. Additional stages focus computation on difficult regions. Multiple crops can require multiple requests.

In the published reference evaluation, double and triple pass add 2.18 and 2.46 ParseBench points over single pass. The additional work lets applications trade some throughput for better extraction in difficult regions. Reference results and serving measurements.

We are sharing a Parse fine-tuning recipe that takes developers through paired data generation, NeMo Automodel SFT, and NeMo RL GRPO, using vLLM to generate candidate answers.

The worked example uses a synthetic dental form with an odontogram: a chart showing teeth, planned procedures, and affected tooth surfaces. Before adaptation, Parse reads the printed tooth numbers but misses the intended procedure table. SFT teaches it to associate each marked tooth with a procedure and its placement on the tooth.

Figure 6. A recorded recipe example: after SFT, all six chart rows match the target. Full image and native training label.

RLVR then reinforces accuracy and consistent completion. In the dental reference run, the estimated first-attempt success rate (sampled pass@1) rose from 0.00% for the base model to 95.85% after SFT and 96.58% after RLVR.

Figure 7. Matched evaluation on 256 held-out forms from the same synthetic generator, with eight samples per page. Success requires natural completion, exact chart content, and error-free normalized page text. Evaluation protocol.

To adapt the recipe, supply your own image/label pairs and a verifier: checks that determine whether an extraction is correct. The included document reward components cover text fidelity, bounding boxes, tables, chart facts, and completion. Combine the components relevant to your task, add schema checks, and use completion and repetition checks to discourage looping or unfinished output.

We are excited that the community has extended and improved Parse for Thai, Persian/Farsi, and Arabic already and we hope that these additional datasets and fine-tuning recipes will help encourage these efforts and future models.

We thank Denis Ovchinnikov for his work on vLLM integration and independent performance validation, Oliver Holworthy for improving the fine-tuning recipe's runtime setup and reproducibility, and Bo Liu for technical review.

#9640. Introducing the llama.cpp benchmark dashboard for AMD Ryzen and Radeon

The llama.cpp × AMD Benchmark dashboard is available on Hugging Face. It lets you track prompt processing and text generation performance across llama.cpp builds, models, and quantizations, so you can explore how local inference performs on AMD Ryzen and Radeon hardware.

Local inference performance changes as models, kernels, and builds evolve. We want those changes to be easy to inspect for any AMD developer: pick a hardware, a model and a build, compare quantizations, and follow performance over time. The benchmark workflow and underlying results are public, so you can also inspect how we benchmark inference performance.

You can choose Hardware, Model, and llama.cpp build in the Configuration sidebar. The current hardware choices are Radeon 8060S (gfx1151) and Radeon AI Pro R9700S (gfx1201).

The dashboard shows two separate tests, both measured in tokens per second:

Both tests start at context depth zero (n_depth=0). PP512 measures processing 512 input tokens without generation; TG128 measures generating 128 tokens without a pre-existing context. The plotted value is the mean throughput (avg_ts). These are useful reference workloads, while the Context scaling tab lets you explore token generation throughput as the context grows.

We benchmark the prebuilt binaries distributed through llama-install.sh, the build and installation project behind llama.app. The public gfx1151 and gfx1201 workflows are scheduled weekly and run the standard benchmarks using the llama-bench tool with Flash Attention on and off, with 10 repetitions per configuration.

The model set evolves and currently includes Inkling 2 Mini, Qwen, Gemma, gpt-oss, and LFM models, covering both dense and mixture-of-experts architectures. Available GGUF formats include Q4_K_M, Q8_0, other quantizations, and higher-precision formats such as BF16 and F16.

The explorer reads directly from the public ggml-org/install.sh-benches-data Storage Bucket on Hugging Face. The data source link beside the chart title opens the folder for the selected build, hardware, and model.

Standard results use ///.jsonl. Workload sweeps use the same folder -tg.jsonl filename.

Use them to investigate a result, make your own charts, or compare with a local run.

Thanks to the AMD team for providing test infrastructure and helping validate the setup! Try the dashboard, inspect the data, and let us know which models and workloads you would like to see next.

#9637. Taking Trainium3 to the Track: Generating Videos with LTX-2.5

Thanks to our partnership with AWS, we were lucky enough to get access to a Trainium3 machine (trn3.48xlarge, 64 NeuronCores) for a month. We spent most of the month testing Hugging Face models on it, and getting more of them to work.

With five days left, I allowed myself a little fun. When you have a Ferrari, every now and then you want to take it out on the track. So I asked myself: what if I tried to generate videos?

I picked LTX-2.5 from Lightricks, which generates video and sound together. By the end, once the models were loaded, a 10-second clip with sound took 22 to 23 s to generate, on half of the machine. Here is the result.

I had two goals. The first was to see how easy it is to generate videos with diffusers on Trainium3. Not the simple clips from the examples: I wanted to make short films from a script, closer to a real use case, like drafting a movie. The second was performance. I wanted to get close to what you get with CUDA, or with LTX's own API.

For CUDA, I found no real figure to compare against. The only one is LTX's claim of 6.8 s for a 10-second 720p clip on four B200 GPUs, with no detail on how it was measured. So I set CUDA aside and compared with LTX's online API instead, which LTX says makes a 10-second 1080p clip in 23.7 s. In the end, the setup matches it, and even beats it by about a second: 22 to 23 s for a 10-second clip at 2048×1024, once the models are loaded, on half of the machine. Not bad, considering how little time I had to optimize the pipelines.

The input is a film: a JSON list of shots, each with a name and a prompt, much like a storyboard. LTX-2.5 does better with long prompts, so each prompt is a paragraph on the style, the subject, the motion, the camera, the light and the sound. Here is the seal film's file, with the prompts shortened:

Each shot has a name and a prompt, and can have a seed, to keep the take I picked among several. Shots are chained with two keys. This chaining is the point, since prompts alone do not keep a subject from one shot to the next:

A shot can also be trimmed, or have a caption drawn over it.

Making a film from shots works like animation, which has two ways to go. Straight ahead, each shot continues the one before. Pose to pose, you make the key shot first, until you get one you like; then the shots before it end on its first frames (to), and the shots after it start from its last frames (from). When a film builds up to a payoff (the moment everything was leading to), the payoff is the key shot. I found this order by trial and error, and made the seal film pose to pose, starting from iceberg.

The payoff is iceberg: the iceberg rolls over, and its wave drenches the seal. nap, the sleeping seal, ends on the first 9 frames of iceberg (to), so that the seal, the floe and the iceberg stay the same into the payoff. shake starts from the last 25 frames of iceberg (from): the dripping seal shakes off the water and flops down on the floe. The dream is made on its own, and a cut joins it to the rest.

On the diffusers side, three pipelines share the models of LTX-2.5. LTX2Pipeline makes the shots from their prompt alone, and LTX2ConditionPipeline makes the shots that start or end on frames of another shot. These two follow the two-stage distilled recipe of the model card: 8 steps, then the third pipeline, LTX2LatentUpsamplePipeline, upscales the latents ×2 before 3 final steps.

The diffusers pipelines do all of the generation. The film part is about 160 lines of Python on top: read the film file, order the shots so each keyframe exists before the shot that needs it, and cut the frames to hand over; then trim, caption, even out the sound and assemble the film. The code is in dacorvo/video-generation. The films I kept are in the dacorvo/video-generation bucket, with their JSON files: the seal, the fox, and the goat, which trims two of its shots and draws a caption over its payoff.

Out of the box, the model does not run on the NeuronCores: the transformer does not fit on one, and diffusers has no plan to split it. The first attempt that ran (the model card's pipeline, with the transformer split over 4 cores and a few patches) took about 5 min 20 s for a 10-second clip, and the NeuronCores were actually computing for only about 45 s of it. What's more, the target resolution was out of reach.

Getting there took three kinds of work: making the model run on the NeuronCores (requires tensor parallelism), splitting it over more of them (sequence parallelism), and making the host keep up with them.

Most of the fixes below are on the device, and that is where most of the effort went. The biggest end-to-end savings came from the host: the low-hanging fruit, since that is obviously where the waste was.

Three issues were never explained: the transformer compiled as one graph returned NaN at one size, the first shot that ends on keyframes was slow in each new process (even with every graph in the cache), and the latent upsampler fails to load next to the transformer, so it stays on the CPU.

Some of this is being fixed upstream. diffusers#15420 (open) fixes the LTX-2 pipelines, which would make the second workaround above unnecessary. diffusers#14725 (still open) brings tensor and context parallelism into one ParallelConfig, and a _tp_plan for LTX-2.5 is planned.

On the performance side, once the models are loaded, a 10-second 2048×1024 clip with sound takes 22 to 23 s. That rivals LTX's paid API, on half of the instance. A service would keep its processes up, as they take about 3 minutes to load the models, and 80 s for their first clip.

On the feature side, diffusers has what it takes to draft a movie. The shots come from prompts, and keep their subject from one shot to the next by starting or ending on frames of other shots. Takes differ by their seed, and the film file keeps the one I picked. Re-run with the same code and film file, and you get the same film back, byte for byte. A shot can also start from an image, such as a storyboard frame or a character sheet, which the condition pipeline takes the same way as frames (I did not try it in a film).

LTX calls LTX-2.5 a world model, with robotics as an emerging use. Robots, cars and drones learn from videos of what their cameras see, and a world model can make more of them, including events too rare or too risky to film. So I also tried it on real footage, with the same code: a shot can start from the first second of a real camera clip and invent what happens next. One frame was not enough, as the model cannot tell from it how fast things move.

Here is the head camera of a Fourier GR1-T2 humanoid robot (a clip from NVIDIA's GR1-100), looking down at a table. In the real 6-second clip, the robot's left hand picks an orange from a plate and drops it in a tray. The model only sees the first second of that clip (the hands raised, before anything moves) and invents the rest. What really happened, next to its invention:

Same scene, same pick: the model invents the grab on its own, and keeps the table, the hands and the fruit consistent with the real footage. More interesting are the events that did not happen. From the same second, with only the prompt changed, a person leans over and grabs the orange too, and the human hand and the robot hand carry it to the tray together. Five takes, with the real footage first:

The person's gestures and timing differ in each take, and the robot's arm adapts to them. That is the appeal for training: not one continuation of a clip, but a distribution of them, each reproducible from its film file and seed.

The robotics folder of the bucket has the five takes with their JSON files, and a second example from the front camera of a car in a snowstorm (Boreas), where the alternate event is slush thrown on the lens by a passing truck. Asked to make the car accelerate instead, the model kept its speed: the prompt does not override what the first second of footage already implies.

These videos follow prompts, not the robot's or car's commands: a training setup would need generation conditioned on those actions. For that, a team fine-tunes the pre-trained checkpoint of LTX-2.5 on the frames and actions of its own robots.

The Ferrari made it around the track, on half of its cylinders.

#9634. How I Built a First-Party Analytics Platform With Next.js Edge Middleware

Design engineer, AI product engineer and founder of Lunar Computing. I build products and write about the decisions underneath them.

Design engineer, AI product engineer and founder of Lunar Computing. I build products and write about the decisions underneath them.

Design engineer, AI product engineer and founder of Lunar Computing. I build products and write about the decisions underneath them.

Every third-party analytics tool has the same shape: a JavaScript snippet in the page, a beacon request back to a data collection endpoint, a dashboard that reads from their database. It works. It also adds a 20-50 KB script to every page, one extra network round trip, a tempting target for ad blockers, and a consent banner because the tool is now a third party processing user data.

None of that is necessary. Next.js Edge Middleware runs on every request, on Vercel's edge network, before the page is served. If you capture analytics there, you have:

Glint is what you get when you take this seriously. The middleware captures the analytics in the same edge function that routes the response, and writes the data to a Postgres table you own. The dashboard reads from the same Postgres. There is no separate analytics service, no SaaS bill, no cross-domain script.

Next.js middleware is a single file at src/middleware.ts. It runs on every request that matches its config.matcher path. For a normal page load, that means it fires once, and it has full access to the request headers.

Every idea that matters about this is in the snippet above. Let me pull them out.

You do not need MaxMind. You do not need a GeoIP database. Vercel's edge network runs an IP lookup against its own tables and injects the result into headers before your middleware sees the request. x-vercel-ip-city, x-vercel-ip-country, and x-vercel-ip-region are present on every edge request at zero cost and zero latency.

The equivalent lookup from a Node server would cost either a paid API call or a GeoIP database file shipped with your deployment. Vercel's inclusion of these headers is one of those platform features that you only notice when you stop using them.

The country header is the single most useful field in the data model. Country plus referrer is enough to answer almost every early-stage analytics question, and it costs a header read.

The obvious risk of tracking in middleware is that any millisecond spent in middleware is a millisecond added to every page's time to first byte. So the tracking must not block the response.

The pattern is Promise.all(...).catch(() => {}) without an await. The fetch requests are kicked off, their promises enter the event loop, and the middleware returns NextResponse.next() immediately. The page renders while the analytics request is still in flight.

On Vercel's edge runtime, background fetches persist for a bounded time after the response is returned. This gives the tracking request long enough to complete without blocking anything user-visible. If the analytics endpoint is slow or down, the page still serves in the normal time. The .catch(() => {}) swallows any error so a failed analytics request cannot surface as a page error.

The trade-off is that in the rare case where the edge function is killed before the background fetch completes, you lose that one event. This is acceptable for analytics, which is inherently sampled. It would not be acceptable for a write that the user was waiting on.

Middleware runs on every matched request. The matcher must exclude everything that is not an actual page view, or you get exponential noise:

The negative lookahead regex /((?!_next|api|favicon.ico).*) excludes these while still matching every real page. This is also the one file in a project where the regex matters: get it wrong and your analytics double or your database fills up with asset noise. There is no easy retry; the data is already dirty.

Glint fires four payloads per request: an "average" record with the user agent data, a location record, a referral record, and a traffic record. Each one goes to the same trackAnalytics endpoint and lands in a different aggregation. This shape is load-bearing for the dashboard, because the queries it drives are grouped differently:

Splitting them on write means the read-side queries never have to group-by on columns that are cheap to pre-aggregate on insert. The dashboard loads in a few milliseconds because the queries are aggregating over pre-shaped rows, not filtering a firehose.

The events table is small. A text column for each major field, a timestamp, a B-tree index on (timestamp, path). Aggregations use date_trunc for time bucketing. Postgres handles this fine into the millions of events; most queries finish in under 50 ms.

Track single-page-app route changes. Next.js App Router handles soft navigations without a new request, which means the middleware never fires for a client-side route change. If you care about per-view tracking inside a SPA, you still need a small client-side beacon.

Track interaction events. Time on page, scroll depth, form abandonment, video completion: all of these are client-side. Edge middleware only sees the initial request.

For most indie products, these limits are acceptable. The 80% use case is "how many people are hitting my site, from where, through what." Edge middleware nails that one, and it nails it without a third-party script, a beacon request, or a consent banner.

The analytics industry has spent a decade training us to accept that tracking costs a script tag and a beacon. It does not. The capability was always on the server: every request already knows who is asking, from where, with what headers. The only reason we put analytics in the client was that we did not have a cheap server-side place to put it. We have one now.

The other thing this proves is that first-party analytics, owned by you, in a database you control, with a dashboard you built, is an order of magnitude simpler than the SaaS version. Glint is under 2000 lines of code. The dashboard charts are divs rendered with computed widths. The whole product would fit inside a weekend if you already had the middleware idea.

The third-party analytics market exists partly because nobody noticed edge middleware made the problem trivial.

How I Built a Self-Hosted Alternative to LaunchDarkly in 300 Lines of Code

By recording any kind of information—such as bank account transactions, the ownership of Non-Fungible Tokens (NFTs), or Decentralized Finance (DeFi) smart contracts—in one place, and distributing it to many different computers, blockchains ensure that data can’t be manipulated without everyone in the system being aware.

The value of an NFT comes from its ability to be traded freely and securely on the blockchain, which is not possible with other current digital ownership solutionsThe NFT points to its location on the blockchain, but doesn’t necessarily contain the digital property. If you buy a non-fungible item, such as a movie ticket, it is impossible to replace it with any other movie ticket because each ticket is unique to a specific time and place.

NFTs also contain smart contracts—small computer programs that run on the blockchain—that give the artist, for example, a cut of any future sale of the token.

#9628. I Tested Google's ARTEMIS: Can AI Agents Really Automate Android Testing?

Software Architect, AI Engineer & Technical Leader. Building apps, exploring dev tools, sharing insights from a decade in tech.

Software Architect, AI Engineer & Technical Leader. Building apps, exploring dev tools, sharing insights from a decade in tech.

Software Architect, AI Engineer & Technical Leader. Building apps, exploring dev tools, sharing insights from a decade in tech.

A reel went around this week claiming Google had quietly open-sourced a tool called ARTEMIS that lets Claude Code, Codex or Cursor drive an Android phone. The claims: about 15k GitHub stars, 99% success on 100+ real phone tasks, it opens apps, taps and types, it tests your app after every change and hands back a report with screenshots and logs.

My team ships Android apps, and the slowest part of every change is still someone tapping through the same five screens on a device. If an agent in my editor can do that for me, I want it. But I don't trust star counts or success rates from a 30-second video, so I cloned the repo, booted an emulator on a Linux box and ran it.

Short version: the project is real, the numbers in the reel are a little off, and it did every job I gave it. The most useful thing I found was a failure mode, not a feature.

The repo is github.com/google/artemis, Apache-2.0, written in Python. It was created on 13 August 2026 and had 17,876 stars and 1,989 forks when I checked on 22 November 2026. The README pitches it as "Let AI assistants and test suites use real phones like a human."

Under the hood it's a LangGraph agent that reads the screen through Android's accessibility tree (it installs its own small Accessibility Helper APK on the device, with UIAutomator2 as the fallback), looks at screenshots with a vision model, and acts through ADB. You can drive it four ways: a web console, a CLI, a Python SDK, and an MCP server, which is the part the reel was about.

I used a Debian box with 8 vCPUs and 15 GB of RAM, with nested KVM available. /dev/kvm existed but my user couldn't open it, so I gave it a temporary ACL and took it away when I was done. With KVM working, a headless Android 14 emulator is straightforward:

The official path is ./start.sh, which also installs ADB, scrcpy and FFmpeg and offers to wire up your IDEs. I went the manual route so I could see each piece. doctor came back "Ready (optional gaps)". The Gemini key was detected, the emulator was connected at 1080x2400, and scrcpy was missing, which only turns off video replay.

My first task failed after three minutes with LLM call timed out after 180 seconds. The logs were full of Gemini 503s ("This model is currently experiencing high demand"). The default config points every node at gemini-3.8-flash, falling back to gemini-3.7-flash, and both were overloaded right then. A separate preset in the same file names gemini-2.5-flash, which now returns 404 for new users.

The fix is three lines in config/artemis.jsonc:

Plus the history-chunking model further down. After that, everything ran. If you put this in CI, pin a model you know you have capacity on, and use a fallback from a different model family, not just the next version down.

It finished in 28 seconds, including spawning the background daemon, in three turns: launch Settings, tap the Battery row, report "The current battery level is 100%." adb shell dumpsys battery agreed: level 100. It made 5 model calls.

This is the bit that matters for coding agents. The server is a FastMCP app you launch over stdio:

The Claude config it prints is just .venv/bin/python -m mcp_server with PYTHONPATH set. For Codex it writes a TOML block with startup_timeout_sec = 120.

I didn't have Claude Code or Codex on this box, so I wrote a small Python MCP client that launches the server the same way those configs do and calls the tools directly. Same transport, same server, same tool calls. It shows exactly what an editor agent sees:

The server reported itself as artemis 1.29.0 and listed five tools:

Their descriptions and schemas add up to 17,696 characters. That's context your agent loads on every session whether it touches a phone or not, so I'd only enable this server in projects that need it.

mobile_diagnose with probe_device=true came back in 1.6 seconds: 5 of 5 required checks passed, the device probe saw 24 elements, and the hierarchy came from the helper. The hierarchy view is compact and agent-friendly. Here's the Battery screen:

Goal: "Open Settings, go to Display and turn on Dark theme, then confirm Dark theme is on."

mobile_manage_task reported completed after 20.2 seconds. That's about 3 seconds per step, which matches the README. I didn't trust the agent's word for it: adb shell cmd uimode night said "Night mode: no" before the run and "Night mode: yes" after. It made 9 model calls.

It also handled its starting point well. The phone was still on the Battery page from Task 1, so its first move was to go back rather than relaunch Settings.

Goal: "Open the Contacts app, create a new contact named Ada Lovelace with mobile number 555-0100, save it, and verify the contact shows up in the contacts list. Report the steps you took."

The Planner wrote a three-milestone plan with a verify item ("contact details saved successfully") and an assert@end ("contact 'Ada Lovelace' is visible in the contacts list"). The Operator then launched Contacts, skipped the Google sign-in promo, tapped +, typed Ada, Lovelace and 555-0100 into the right fields, saved, and navigated back to the list. The first seven actions came 6 to 8 seconds apart. The last two took longer because of more 503 retries.

The work was real. The contacts provider had the row:

Then the final review ran. By that point my Gemini key, which was on the free tier, had used up its daily limit of 20 requests for gemini-3.6-flash. The Checker's call came back 429, and ARTEMIS logged this:

So the MCP status said completed, with a test_summary of 0 passed and 2 inconclusive. The device state was correct. But if I had wired this into a pipeline that only checked status == "completed", a run whose verifier never ran would have gone green.

That's a design choice, and the data is there: test_summary is machine-readable and clearly says inconclusive: 2. You just have to read it. If you use ARTEMIS as a test gate, fail on anything other than failed == 0 and inconclusive == 0, and run with verification_level="checkpoints" or "strict" so the asserts are checked along the way, not just once at the exit.

Pro also costs more. This run took 360 seconds and 26 model calls, and ARTEMIS's own usage log shows about 4.5 times the prompt volume of the Flash dark-theme run, for a task with nine actions.

The README's leaderboard chart puts ARTEMIS at 99.1% Pass@1 on AndroidWorld's 116 tasks. FinalRun is next at 97.4%, the human baseline is 80.0%, and Gemini 2.5 Computer Use sits at 69.7%. AndroidWorld is a solid benchmark: 116 hand-crafted tasks, instantiated with random parameters on a live emulator, with durable reward signals. But this chart is ARTEMIS's own, the repo doesn't ship the eval harness or say which model and profile produced the number, and AndroidWorld runs on an emulator. "99% on real phones" isn't what it says.

What I can say from three tasks: three out of three were done correctly on the device, and I checked each one with adb rather than trusting the agent's report. That's a sanity check, not a benchmark.

The pattern ARTEMIS's own rules file pushes is the right one. The coding agent uses ARTEMIS to explore the app and find the real path through the UI, then writes a deterministic test (Espresso, UIAutomator, Maestro, whatever you use) that runs without a model in the loop. The mobile_run_task docs say it outright: "run once to discover the path, then author a deterministic script."

That's also my answer to the "automates repetitive tasks" claim. It can, but paying for a model call and about 3 seconds per step, every time, is the expensive way to repeat something.

For a smoke check after a change ("build, install, log in, tell me if anything weird pops up"), Flash is fast enough to stay in the edit loop. For anything you'll gate a merge on, use Pro with checkpoint verification, pin a model you have capacity on, and read test_summary instead of status.

Then ask your agent to open your app on the emulator and tell you what it sees.

#9625. Can AI agents maintain our software architecture documentation?

With the advent of AI, documentation has taken a more important place than before. First, as we delegate more and more coding tasks to AI agents and we switch context a lot faster than before, it's easier to forget decisions. Second, AI is also a lot better at writing documentation so delegating it means we also don't have a hand in that anymore.

But we still need to have access to the docs, the RFC and the ADR, written in order to know how the system is and how we got there. In this article, we'll explore a setup with Claude and Obsidian in order to maintain a project's documentation and see how it looks like. So in this article, I'll explore with you how I'm trying to set this up.

I will be using my side project Notifizz as an example. We have a few developers working on it, taking decisions with their own AI agents and modifying the code. Right now, the documentation in our project looks something like this inside our repository:

As of today, we have around 160 ADR, 45 RFC and about 300 plans that we generated with an agent. It's a good start but we lack a clear overview of each domain and we don't really know easily when an ADR stopped being right, or what is the status of our decisions.

Obsidian is a free application used to take notes and manage knowledge databases.

For my purposes, I'm going to create an Obsidian Vault, a local system folder to store my markdown files and a hidden .obsidian configuration folder for app settings and plugins.

Once you've installed the application, you can find the "Obsidian Vault" button on the bottom left, then "Manage Vaults...". In the modal, you can create your new vault and choose a folder from which to store your vault.

What I'm hoping is that Obsidian is going to give us an easier interface to work with, by displaying properties and allowing us to filter them (domain, verified_at, reviewed_on...). Also, Obsidian has backlinks and graphs that should work nicely with our markdowns.

I chose one of our most complex domains to test it out: notification tracking. Notification tracking is how Notifizz knows what happens to a notification after it is sent.

Once that's done (and after fixing some formatting issues), I end up with an index page with a table that gives me an overview of each domain and its status (confronted with the code, did I review it, how fresh it is ... )

In each domain, I get a page called map, that explains to me in a rather succinct Markdown document what the domain contains and how it does it. The properties include the domain, a sha for the verified_at, a title and a list of sources used. The sources include the ADR, RFC and the code that Claude consulted. So, it's a photograph of what the code contains at that moment.

The second page is called decisions. This one lists the ADRs of this domain and check if the code applies it. So this page is more about realizing the differences between the decisions we took and the state of the code. The page has several tables for each ADR of the domain and describes the gaps between the ADR and the code.

Ok, I could see this being somewhat useful. But so far, I'm not entirely convinced.

Using the "Bases" functionality, I can display a table with filters, the properties list, a search functionality. Now we're talking. Obviously, it's not very useful now because I have only two domains but down the line, I can see this being quite good.

In the decisions pages, Claude added a little diagram that allows me to have a quick overview of the decisions and their status for this domain. That feels better than a table.

A weekly scheduled task checks the knowledge base against the latest code. It flags the pages whose code has changed, lists any new ADRs or RFCs, and drafts an update for one page on a separate branch. I don't want the agent to modify the knowledge base by itself. I review the diff and merge it. I want to have the final say.

The "one page" is important I believe, I don't want to be drowned in updates. I don't think this project has enough people to have that many changes that would require a big update change regularly. I'll see after a few weeks if the knowledge base become too much behind the reality.

Claude, after running the tasks, gives me a table of proposed changes to modify the docs. I've asked for checkboxes on each modification so I can cherry-pick which one I want or not.

The initial setup is, I think, decent. I'm gonna ask Claude to map 2 or 3 more domains of my project to see how it looks.

Right off the bat, we have 6 gaps that appeared on the notification tracking domain. Things that we decided in the latest ADR doesn't appear that way in the code, or at least partially. So, I have a pretty clear list of things to check. Why do we have those gaps? Are those decisions that we took during the implementation of the code with Claude and we decided to deviate from the ADR? Or is there a clear problem that we need to address? Or did Claude misinterpreted something.

The first 3 gaps seem to be a lack of implementation, but I don't a reason as for why it's not in the code. That would need some extra analysis. But at least, I know where to look.

As a reminder, the goal of this experiment was to do a little proof-of-concept to have an agent maintain my project's knowledge base. Because we don't write much code today, and we are switching contexts very rapidly, it's easy to feel like the project is slipping out of our hands and not ours anymore.

The test was to use Obsidian to have a better interface to consult the hundreds of documents that we have. What is interesting in my case is really two things:

This first overview gives me a clearer picture of where I'm standing. I feel like the domain recap gives me an opportunity to learn parts of the application I haven't touched yet. And having the lists of gaps between the code and the ADRs maintained automatically by an agent is useful to keep track of what needs to be done.

Overall, for a setup that took me a couple hours to set up, it feels nice. Obviously, I'm gonna need a few weeks of trial, testing and adjustments to make sure this tool fits our needs. But reading it feels a lot less overwhelming than searching through hundreds of markdown files in an editor.

There is a clear risk to this approach that I have to be careful about: AI-driven documentation sprawl. While code usually passes code reviews and CI tests, documentation rarely has that sort of checks. AI can create a huge mass of documentation that is impossible to review for humans. Obsolete documentation can become an issue for agentic workflows because your agents are using wrong data to write code or propose solutions. In this case, documentation becomes more a problem than an assistance.

So, this is why I chose a weekly review that doesn't modify anything without my approval to mitigate this. I feel like documentation becomes more important than ever and I need to have a say in it, I need to stay in control of what makes it to the documentation. If that becomes a source for our agentic workflows to fix bugs or develop new feature, it needs to be precise.

I now have an Obsidian vault that keeps tracks of domains in my Notifizz project. I have an overview of what these domains do in the code and possible gaps between the decisions taken in the ADRs and the code. In the future, an agent runs every week to check if new things have been done and if the documentation may be obsolete. But, in order to avoid the docs to become false, I'll keep the final word.

It's going to take me some time to refine, test it, talk about it with my colleagues to find the right tuning for this tool. But I have a feeling this could become something useful in the future.

Do you use special tools or agentic workflows to keep track of your documentation in your projects?

#9623. Moving Proof-of-Assay’s Explanation Layer to Nosana With Ollama and Qwen2.5

AI and Blockchain developer with domain focus on Corporate finance and supply chain applications

AI and Blockchain developer with domain focus on Corporate finance and supply chain applications

AI and Blockchain developer with domain focus on Corporate finance and supply chain applications

I got an email from the hackathon team this week: Proof-of-Assay had been shortlisted for the Decentralized Compute track in Round 2 of HackerNoon's Decentralize AI Hackathon, and there was a $70 credit to put an open model on their network. I claimed it on the same account I'd used for an earlier Nosana run. This is what I did with it, including the part that didn't work at first.

I'm Shyam, a CFO who works in junior mining finance. Proof-of-Assay is a small audit agent for a problem I actually have: reconciling assay certificates with supplier invoices, lot by lot, and leaving a receipt that someone else can re-verify later.

The verdicts are decided by plain Python rules, not by a language model. Expected amount is tonnes times the contracted price. Grade, quantity, and amount mismatches get flagged and priced as cash at risk. Every decision goes into a SHA-256 hash chain. Anyone can run two commands on a laptop and get the same 11-entry chain, ending at 907c7041a4a27a44941acf90699a019c8cfe08b0eb4d3f7ef9c3636c8c6cd5ac:

The model has one job: write a short explanation of a verdict the rules already made. I learned why that split matters in October, when I asked a 1.5B Qwen model on Nosana whether a low assay was CLEAN or an EXCEPTION, and it said CLEAN with complete confidence. It was wrong. So this time I didn't ask the model to audit anything. I asked it to explain work the rules had already finished.

Synthetic-data disclosure: The eight mining lots in this post are fictional demo fixtures. Amounts are deterministic fixture arithmetic, not real mine payables. Proof-of-Assay is a prototype, not a production auditor.

Because I don't want that layer to depend on a single AI vendor's API. If the narration is an open-weight model I can start on a rented GPU, I can move it, pin the image, and keep the deterministic core exactly as it is. The audit still runs when the GPU is off; you just don't get the paragraphs. For this hackathon, Nosana was the natural place to host that model, and HackerNoon asked for a progress post. This is that post.

The setup is a single container. The image is docker.io/ollama/ollama:0.32.6, pinned, serving qwen2.5:7b — Ollama's default 4-bit instruct build, 4.68 GB on disk, 7.6 billion parameters, Q4_K_M. The API is OpenAI-compatible at /v1/chat/completions, which is what proof_of_assay/llm.py calls when NOSANA_LLM_BASE_URL is set. If that environment variable is missing, the audit still produces the same chain and the narratives are skipped.

I wanted a cheaper card first. On November 11, 2026, the NVIDIA 4070 premium market was about $0.10 an hour, and the 3090 premium market — the same one I used in October — was $0.19. I planned a Simple deployment, one replica, with a short container timeout, and I was ready to stop it as soon as the demo was done. The 4070 hosts were all busy, so I took an RTX 3090 at $0.19 an hour. The dashboard's create page also no longer offered the 60-minute auto-stop I had wanted, so the job was set to run to completion with a six-hour cap — about $1.14 if I let it sit. After the $70 shortlist credit, the account had $209.83 to work with. I didn't add a card, and I didn't connect a wallet.

The current job definition is in the repo at nosana/proof-of-assay-llm.json.

The first job definition used a resources entry of type Ollama to preload qwen2.5:7b. The container came up healthy. GET /api/tags returned 200. The model list was empty.

That tracks with the docs, once I went back and looked. Official Nosana resource types are S3 and Hugging Face, not a first-class Ollama preload. The documented way to stand up an Ollama endpoint is the obvious one: start the server, then pull the model.

On the live deployment, I pulled it by hand with POST /api/pull. The job definition in the repo now follows that pattern, and it waits until ollama list succeeds instead of sleeping for a fixed five seconds:

If I start this job again, I shouldn't need the manual pull. I didn't redeploy this run just to prove it — the 3090 was already serving the model, and I didn't want to pay for another startup.

Once the model was on the card, I pointed the audit at it and ran the same script anyone can run:

python scripts/verify_chain.py printed chain_length=11 verification=PASS. The chain head is the same value the fixtures produce with no model in the loop. Narratives are written onto the results for display. They are not hashed into the receipt.

I also timed the eight explanation calls separately, using the same prompts the client sends, at 1:43 PM Eastern on November 11, 2026. A first request, made after the model had been pulled but wasn't in VRAM, took 4.010 seconds to return a three-token reply. The eight lot explanations then finished in 10.975 seconds of wall time — 1.371 seconds each on average, ranging from 1.231 to 1.505 seconds. Together they used 1,877 prompt tokens and 712 completion tokens, 2,589 in total. These are measurements from one afternoon on one 3090, not a benchmark.

The explanations are plain, and they stay on the numbers they were given. On LOT-003, the grade mismatch, Qwen wrote:

The audit identified an exception for Lot ID LOT-003 due to a significant variance in the invoiced amount of $893,174.00 compared to the expected amount of $760,693.50, resulting in a cash at risk of $132,480.50. Additionally, there was a grade mismatch between the invoice grade of 2.85 g/t and the assay grade of 2.41 g/t, further complicating the discrepancy.

The audit identified an exception for LOT-006 due to a variance of $98,215.44 between the invoiced amount ($604,903.44) and the expected amount ($506,688.00). Additionally, there is a quantity mismatch with 1126 tonnes invoiced versus the contracted 960 tonnes. These discrepancies are causing the status to be marked as "EXCEPTION."

The audit identified an exception for Lot ID LOT-007, where the invoiced amount of $374,897.25 does not match the expected amount of $315,744.00, resulting in a variance of $59,153.25. This discrepancy is reflected in the high cash at risk of $59,153.25 and has been flagged as an exception due to the significant difference between the expected and invoiced amounts.

That's useful for a reviewer. It is also still a paraphrase of rules that already ran. I would not replace verify_chain.py with any of those paragraphs, and I'm not going to claim the 7B model is a better auditor than the 1.5B model I asked to decide a verdict in October. It's doing a different job: narrating a decision it was not allowed to make.

I'll leave this deployment up long enough for a short demo video and this post, then stop it so the credits don't keep ticking at $0.19 an hour. The job-definition fix is in the public repo, so the next start should pull qwen2.5:7b on its own. I want to keep this pattern — an open model I host, and a core that doesn't care whether the model is there — for later work that needs a short explanation layer. I am not putting the model on the verdict path.

The code, the job definition, a static verifier, and the demo video are public:

This is a prototype. The lots are fictional. The useful result is that I could move the explanation step onto a decentralized GPU without moving the receipt.

#9621. Prioritize CVE-2026-133311 as part of an exploited MiCollab cluster

A vulnerability management queue can make CVE-2026-133311 look easy to defer. Mitel rates the MiCollab AWV issue 5.9, describes a high-complexity attack and limits the direct impact to sensitive information disclosure. The CVE alone does not receive a critical score. The surrounding evidence changes the priority. The same advisory contains command-execution issues, the five-CVE set has been exploited, and CISA ADP marks exploitation as active.

That is not an argument for treating every medium issue as critical. It is an argument for grouping related findings when the vendor and attackers treat them as a set. A patch program that ranks each CVE in isolation may postpone the authentication flaw while a critical sibling is remediated. If both are fixed by the same advisory and affect the same component, splitting the work can leave a prepared or partially patched path behind.

Record the CVE's own facts first. CVE-2026-133311 is CWE-1390 weak authentication, affects MiCollab through 10.3 (10.3.0.18), requires a specific generated identifier or pre-staged content, and can disclose sensitive information. The CVSS 3.1 vector is network reachable, high complexity, no privileges and no user interaction, with high confidentiality impact only. Mitel's patch for 10.3.0.18 or a later supported release is the remediation path.

Then record the portfolio context. MISA-2026-0012 includes CVE-2026-133275, CVE-2026-133303, CVE-2026-133311, CVE-2026-133323 and CVE-2026-133324. The first, second, fourth and fifth cover upload, XML injection, command injection and authentication bypass. Mitel says exploiting them together can significantly amplify impact. CERT-In reports known exploitation. APEX Labs published an intrusion timeline and CISA KEV references.

The risk record should describe both levels. It should not claim that the medium CVE alone caused the critical outcome. It should explain why the same exposed component and patch cycle create a common remediation boundary.

Is the affected component reachable from the internet or from an untrusted partner network? Does the server integrate with Active Directory or store credentials for other systems? Is the version at or below 10.3.0.18? Has the vendor patch been verified rather than assumed from a build label? Are upstream logs available and retained long enough to investigate exploitation before the patch window?

If AWV is externally reachable and the version is unpatched, contain first and investigate immediately. If the component is not externally reachable, still apply the vendor fix and verify that no secondary path exists through a proxy or gateway. The CVSS score informs severity, but reachability, identity integration and known exploitation set the operational timeline.

The CVE record's CISA ADP entry references the Accenture report and the KEV catalog, and its SSVC content marks exploitation as active. SecurityWeek reports that all five MiCollab flaws were added to KEV. APEX Labs observed a web shell before Mitel published the advisory and reported a second server communicating with the same actor infrastructure.

ZoomEye returned 730,707 matches for http.body="MiCollab" and zero matches for vul.cve="CVE-2026-133311". The page-body count indicates a broad searchable product presence, not a confirmed vulnerable population. It should not be used as a risk multiplier by itself. Internal inventory and version evidence are more defensible.

Define completion as a supported patched build, verified on every production node, with all publication paths accounted for. Apply the 10.3.0.18 patch or move to a later release. Restrict external AWV access until validation is complete. Preserve evidence from systems that may have been compromised before the patch.

After remediation, review the LDAP connector and other reachable secrets. Examine proxy and identity logs for pre-patch activity. If the organization uses a KEV deadline, track the application patch and the incident investigation as separate workstreams. Closing the vulnerability ticket does not close a possible intrusion.

The priority statement should be concise: CVE-2026-133311 is a medium authentication flaw in an actively exploited multi-CVE MiCollab set. Remediate it with its sibling CVEs and treat exposed, unpatched servers as potential compromise cases.

When you sign up for an account, Canva will suggest different post types to choose from. Next, you can choose a template. Choose from hundreds of templates that are ready to go, with customizable photos, text, and other elements.

The Photos tab lets you search for and choose from millions of professional stock photos for your templates.

Once you have chosen a video, you can use the editing features in Canva to trim the video, flip it, and adjust its transparency.

On the Background tab, you’ll find free stock photos to serve as backgrounds on your designs. Change out the background on a template to give it a more personal touch.

The Styles tab lets you quickly change the look and feel of your template with just a click. And if you have a Canva Pro subscription, you can upload your brand’s custom colors and fonts to ensure designs stay on brand.

With Canva, free users can download and share designs to multiple platforms including Instagram, Facebook, Twitter, LinkedIn, Pinterest, Slack and Tumblr.

In addition to mobile apps, you can use Canva’s integration with other Internet services to add images and text from sources like Google Maps, Emojis, photos from Google Drive and Dropbox, YouTube videos, Flickr photos, Bitmojis, and other popular visual content elements.

In general, Canva is an excellent tool for those who need simple images for projects. If you are a graphic designer with experience, you will find Canva’s platform lacking in customization and advanced features – particularly vectors. But if you have little design experience, you will find Canva easier to use than advanced graphic design tools like Adobe Photoshop or Illustrator for most projects. #9616. A Cereal Box Whistle Once Hacked AT&T. Your AI Agent Has the Same Bug

Independent legal researcher exploring AI security, cybersecurity, cyber law, digital evidence, and technology governance.

Independent legal researcher exploring AI security, cybersecurity, cyber law, digital evidence, and technology governance.

Independent legal researcher exploring AI security, cybersecurity, cyber law, digital evidence, and technology governance.

In the late 1960s, a toy whistle from a box of Cap'n Crunch could get you free long-distance calls.

Cover one of its two holes, blow, and it made a 2600 Hz tone. AT&T's long-distance trunks used that exact tone to mean "this line is idle." Play it into the mouthpiece and the switch at the far end decided the call was over, then sat there waiting for routing instructions from whoever was still on the line. Which was you.

The whistle wasn't the real flaw. The flaw was that AT&T sent its control signals down the same channel as your voice, so anything that could make the right noise could give orders. Engineers call that in-band signaling. Phone phreaks called it a free call to anywhere.

AT&T couldn't patch its way out. Changing the tones only bought time. The fix was to rebuild the network so control signals traveled on a separate channel that customers couldn't reach, and that work ran into the 1980s.

I bring this up because we've rebuilt the same flaw from scratch, in software, and wired it to our inboxes, our repos and our payment tools. Bruce Schneier made this comparison back in 2024. Two years later it reads less like an analogy and more like an incident report.

Strip away the product and a large language model does one thing. It takes a long sequence of tokens (chunks of text) and predicts which token comes next. Then it does that again.

Everything the model knows about your request sits in that one sequence, called the context window. Your system prompt goes in. The user's message goes in. So does the PDF you asked it to summarize, the web page it fetched, and the output of the tool it just called.

We like to picture these as layers with different ranks. Developer instructions on top, the user in the middle, documents at the bottom as inert data. The model sees no such thing. Chat formats add role markers, and training teaches the model to favor the system prompt, but that's a habit it picked up. Nothing in the software enforces it. There's no privilege bit. A sentence inside a scraped web page is made of the same stuff as a sentence from you.

The UK's National Cyber Security Centre said as much last December when it described LLMs as inherently confusable. A model that follows an instruction buried in a document hasn't malfunctioned. Following plausible-looking text is the job.

Direct prompt injection is the version everyone has seen. You type "ignore your previous instructions" into a chatbot and it does something its owner never planned for.

The famous one is the car dealership bot that agreed to sell a Chevy Tahoe for one dollar, after a visitor told it to agree with whatever the customer said. It was funny. Nobody drove home in a Tahoe.

Damage in those years topped out at a screenshot. The attacker and the user were the same person, the model could only produce text, and the worst outcome was a red-faced brand. Plenty of teams filed prompt injection under "PR risk" and moved on.

I think that filing decision is why so many people are underprepared now.

Indirect prompt injection drops the assumption that the person typing is the attacker. The instructions arrive inside something the model was asked to read. An email. A web page. A PDF, a calendar invite, a code comment. The user asks an innocent question, the model picks up the planted text along the way, and it has no way to tell that text apart from the task.

Researchers described this on paper in early 2023. The proof that it works against a shipping product came in June 2025, with EchoLeak.

Aim Security found that one crafted email, sent to someone using Microsoft 365 Copilot, could make Copilot pull data from that person's organization and ship it to the attacker. The victim didn't have to click anything. The email just had to sit in the inbox until Copilot swept it up as context. Microsoft scored the bug 9.3 out of 10 and fixed it on its own servers.

Now reread that with the whistle in mind. An outsider with no account and no password pushed some text into a channel the system was listening on, and the system took it as an order.

A chatbot that gets injected says something dumb. An agent that gets injected does something. Models now read mail, browse, run shell commands, open pull requests, and move money, usually with their owner's credentials. So the attack surface is anything the agent might read.

In March, Palo Alto's Unit 42 reported injections on live websites and counted 22 distinct techniques for hiding them. One scam page carried hidden text aimed at the AI system reviewing its ad. Others tried to talk agents into sending $5,000 through a PayPal link, or into deleting a database.

In April came "Comment and Control." Researchers showed that text planted in a pull request title or an issue comment could steer Claude Code Security Review, Gemini CLI Action and GitHub Copilot Agent into leaking tokens and API keys from the workflows they ran in.

In June, a team at Tenet fed fabricated Sentry error events to coding agents and got them to run attacker-chosen commands in 85% of controlled tests. Sit with that one for a second. Your error tracker is an input field now.

Then email, again. This summer Straiker showed an agent on Google's Antigravity platform reading a fake "Company Backup" email, hunting down SSH keys on the machine and uploading them. There was a human in the loop, and the human approved it. The dialog only said the agent wanted to run a script called gmail.py.

I want to be straight about scale, because security writing tends to skip this part. When Google scanned billions of crawled pages for injections, most of what turned up was pranks, SEO tricks and site owners trying to shoo AI crawlers away. The malicious slice grew 32% between November 2025 and February 2026, but Google's own read was that the attacks were crude and looked like individuals experimenting.

I don't find that comforting. Crude attempts against a flaw nobody can patch is how most exploit classes begin. By July, Proofpoint was reporting injection kits for emails, PDFs and calendar invites advertised to criminals from about $150 a month, though much of it was still experimental.

The comparison most developers reach for is SQL injection. We solved that one, right?

We did, and the way we solved it is the bad news. SQL injection ended, wherever people bothered, with parameterized queries. The database receives the query and the data through separate doors, and nothing that comes in through the data door can ever run as code. That's out-of-band signaling. Same idea the phone company landed on.

An LLM has one door. There is no parameterized prompt. You can wrap untrusted text in tags and tell the model "this part is data, don't obey it," and it helps a bit, but you're asking the confused party to please stop being confused. The NCSC's view is that prompt injection may never be fully mitigated the way SQL injection was, and that products claiming to stop it deserve suspicion.

Filters share the weakness. A classifier that catches 95% of injections sounds great until you remember the attacker gets unlimited tries. Simon Willison, who coined the term prompt injection, says it bluntly: in web security, 95% is a failing grade.

Assume the model will be fooled at some point. Then ask what it's able to do in that moment.

The best one-line test I know is Willison's lethal trifecta. An agent is dangerous when it has all three at once: access to private data, exposure to attacker-controlled content, and a way to send data out. Take away any one and the theft has nowhere to go. Meta's Agents Rule of Two widens the third leg to cover changing state at all, so it also catches the agent that deletes things or spends money.

In practice, this turns into fairly boring engineering.

Injection will still happen with all of this in place. It'll just have far less to work with.

You don't need a fleet of coding agents for any of this to apply. If you have a Make.com or Zapier scenario where an LLM step reads inbound email, a support form or a scraped page, you're running an agent. It's a small one, but the same rules bite.

For each automation, write down three things.

Any automation with an answer in all three columns goes to the top of the list. The cheapest fix is usually column three. Put a draft and approve step in front of anything that sends, pays or deletes.

The phone network stayed open to the whistle trick long after the cause was public knowledge. The fix was understood. It also meant replacing equipment that otherwise worked fine, so it dragged on into the 1980s.

LLMs don't have their separate channel yet. People are working on designs that would give them one, and maybe a future architecture carries instructions and data on different wires. I hope so.

Until that ships, every agent you deploy is a long-distance trunk that listens to whoever happens to be on the line. I'd assume anything mine reads can talk back to it, and I'd decide what it's allowed to do with that in mind.

Your AI Agent Has Permissions. Who Gave It the Authority?

#9615. Why Zero-Login, Sub-100ms Web Tools Beat Heavy Apps for Mobile-First STEM Students

Across South Asia and emerging education markets, the biggest barrier to quality university admission preparation is rarely a lack of motivation—it is friction.

Most commercial EdTech platforms follow a familiar playbook: require students to download a 120MB mobile app, create an account with phone verification, and hit a subscription paywall before they can check a single past-year question or eligibility rule. For a high-school student on a budget Android phone and an unstable 4G connection, that friction is often enough to make them give up.

While building Shikka.bd, an open-access university admission and 3D STEM learning hub, we tested the opposite approach: zero-login, sub-100ms web tools designed specifically for mobile-first students.

When a student searches Google at midnight for "DU admission negative marking rules" or "National University merit score calculation", they want an immediate, trustworthy answer—not an app store redirect.

Forcing an app install creates three problems:

Making a web platform fast does not mean stripping away interactivity. On Shikka.bd, we separated discoverable reference content from heavy simulation bundles:

Students preparing for high-stakes exams need verified numbers, not guesses. Every formula, GPA threshold, and negative-marking rule should cite official university circulars clearly and work without requiring personal data or account sign-ups.

When EdTech teams remove login walls and optimize for sub-100ms web delivery, educational access expands immediately—especially for students who rely on shared devices or prepaid mobile data.

#9612. The Grim Reaper reviews my pull requests

Posted on Nov 28 • Edited on Nov 28 • AI-assisted

I wrote this as part of the Kiroween 2026 hackathon.

In an early PartySim build, adding a second drinks table took the simulated wait from three minutes to eight. The build passed.

Every year we throw a Halloween party for about 80 people. I built PartySim for it. Give it a floor plan and it builds a 3D haunted house full of simulated guests, so you can see where the party jams up.

I have a day job, so I set up Kiro Crew on my laptop to work through a queue while I was away. The jobs built changes, reviewed them and opened pull requests. I decided what got merged. Other people call this a software factory. For this project, we call it a haunted house.

Early on I gave three models the same small feature. All three passed the build and linter. In the app, one worked, one was too faint to see, and one did nothing. Even the one that worked left this in its log:

The next night, three more features passed build and lint and still had problems I could see or hear in the app.

For a visual change, the brief names one thing I should be able to see. A script opens the same URL and repeats the same clicks on the branch and on the commit where it split from main. The Grim Reaper reads the brief and the diff, then compares the screenshots. He writes PASS or FAIL with the screenshot and the file and line he checked. His agent is configured to write its findings in one folder:

Back to the drinks table. Guests walking to a table didn't count toward its line, so too many picked the table that looked free. Pull request #6 counted guests on the way over and turned the table so its line ran onto the lawn. At the same minute of the same party, adding the second table now took the wait from three minutes down to two.

On another change, the brief asked for three lines of text to fit. They did. The extra line cut off the bottoms of the buttons below. The build and linter passed. The Reaper wrote FAIL.

Frankenstein picks a ready row and leaves the roadmap at in review on his branch. The screenshot script saves the URL and clicks in shots.json, so the Reaper can replay the builder’s path on both versions of the app.

The Ferryman reads the first verdict in review.md and skips the branch if it says FAIL. Some briefs also ask for an “Unchanged, on purpose” comparison so I can check a screen the fix was supposed to leave alone.

I handed Dracula a request or wrote the brief myself. Frankenstein, the Grim Reaper and the Ferryman ran on timers. They passed work through files and Git: a brief, a branch, screenshots and a review note. I handled the merge.

The prompts and permissions live in .kiro/agents/. The roadmap is Markdown. For 102 of the 110 briefs in the build queue, we wrote out what to find and what to replace. That let me give Frankenstein the work on a small model at 0.06× Kiro credits.

Between November 10 and 25, the Ferryman opened 103 pull requests. The PRs credit Frankenstein with 83 builds. Ninety-nine included screenshots, and 54 had a section for a screen that was supposed to stay the same.

I couldn't review them as fast as they came in. One evening I merged ten in the same second. I still have to work out how to give each one a proper look.

A screenshot also shows one moment. How do you test a queue that only starts backing up ten minutes into a simulation?

I used AI to help edit this post and illustrate the crew.

#9607. Ahrefs vs SEMrush: Which SEO Tool Should You Use?

SEMrush and Ahrefs are among the most popular tools in the SEO industry. Both companies have been in business for years and have thousands of customers per month.

If you're a professional SEO or trying to do digital marketing on your own, at some point you'll likely consider using a tool to help with your efforts. Ahrefs and SEMrush are two names that will likely appear on your shortlist.

In this guide, I'm going to help you learn more about these SEO tools and how to choose the one that's best for your purposes.

SEMrush is a popular SEO tool with a wide range of features—it's the leading competitor research service for online marketers. SEMrush's SEO Keyword Magic tool offers over 20 billion Google-approved keywords, which are constantly updated and it's the largest keyword database.

The program was developed in 2007 as SeoQuake is a small Firefox extension

Ahrefs is a leading SEO platform that offers a set of tools to grow your search traffic, research your competitors, and monitor your niche. The company was founded in 2010, and it has become a popular choice among SEO tools. Ahrefs has a keyword index of over 10.3 billion keywords and offers accurate and extensive backlink data updated every 15-30 minutes and it is the world's most extensive backlink index database.

Now that you know a little more about each tool, let's take a look at how they compare. I'll analyze each tool to see how they differ in interfaces, keyword research resources, rank tracking, and competitor analysis.

Ahrefs and SEMrush both offer comprehensive information and quick metrics regarding your website's SEO performance. However, Ahrefs takes a bit more of a hands-on approach to getting your account fully set up, whereas SEMrush's simpler dashboard can give you access to the data you need quickly.

In this section, we provide a brief overview of the elements found on each dashboard and highlight the ease with which you can complete tasks.

The Ahrefs dashboard is less cluttered than that of SEMrush, and its primary menu is at the very top of the page, with a search bar designed only for entering URLs.

Additional features of the Ahrefs platform include:

When you log into the SEMrush Tool, you will find four main modules. These include information about your domains, organic keyword analysis, ad keyword, and site traffic.

Both Ahrefs and SEMrush have user-friendly dashboards, but Ahrefs is less cluttered and easier to navigate. On the other hand, SEMrush offers dozens of extra tools, including access to customer support resources.

When deciding on which dashboard to use, consider what you value in the user interface, and test out both.

If you're looking to track your website's search engine ranking, rank tracking features can help. You can also use them to monitor your competitors.

Let's take a look at Ahrefs vs. SEMrush to see which tool does a better job.

The Ahrefs Rank Tracker is simpler to use. Just type in the domain name and keywords you want to analyze, and it spits out a report showing you the search engine results page (SERP) ranking for each keyword you enter.

Rank Tracker looks at the ranking performance of keywords and compares them with the top rankings for those keywords. Ahrefs also offers:

You'll see metrics that help you understand your visibility, traffic, average position, and keyword difficulty.

It gives you an idea of whether a keyword would be profitable to target or not.

SEMRush offers a tool called Position Tracking. This tool is a project tool—you must set it up as a new project. Below are a few of the most popular features of the SEMrush Position Tracking tool:

The platform provides opportunities to track several SERP features, including Local tracking.

Intuitive reports allow you to track statistics for the pages on your website, as well as the keywords used in those pages.

Identify pages that may be competing with each other using the Cannibalization report.

Ahrefs is a more user-friendly option. It takes seconds to enter a domain name and keywords. From there, you can quickly decide whether to proceed with that keyword or figure out how to rank better for other keywords.

SEMrush allows you to check your mobile rankings and ranking updates daily, which is something Ahrefs does not offer. SEMrush also offers social media rankings, a tool you won't find within the Ahrefs platform. Both are good which one do you like let me know in the comment.

Keyword research is closely related to rank tracking, but it's used for deciding which keywords you plan on using for future content rather than those you use now.

When it comes to SEO, keyword research is the most important thing to consider when comparing the two platforms.

The Ahrefs Keyword Explorer provides you with thousands of keyword ideas and filters search results based on the chosen search engine.

Ahrefs supports several features, including:

SEMrush's Keyword Magic Tool has over 20 billion keywords for Google. You can type in any keyword you want, and a list of suggested keywords will appear.

Both of these tools offer keyword research features and allow users to break down complicated tasks into something that can be understood by beginners and advanced users alike.

If you're interested in keyword suggestions, SEMrush appears to have more keyword suggestions than Ahrefs does. It also continues to add new features, like the Keyword Gap tool and SERP Questions recommendations.

Both platforms offer competitor analysis tools, eliminating the need to come up with keywords off the top of your head. Each tool is useful for finding keywords that will be useful for your competition so you know they will be valuable to you.

Ahrefs' domain comparison tool lets you compare up to five websites (your website and four competitors) side-by-side.it also shows you how your site is ranked against others with metrics such as backlinks, domain ratings, and more.

Use the Competing Domains section to see a list of your most direct competitors, and explore how many keywords matches your competitors have.

To find more information about your competitor, you can look at the Site Explorer and Content Explorer tools and type in their URL instead of yours.

SEMrush provides a variety of insights into your competitors' marketing tactics. The platform enables you to research your competitors effectively. It also offers several resources for competitor analysis including:

Traffic Analytics helps you identify where your audience comes from, how they engage with your site, what devices visitors use to view your site, and how your audiences overlap with other websites.

SEMrush's Organic Research examines your website's major competitors and shows their organic search rankings, keywords they are ranking for, and even if they are ranking for any (SERP) features and more.

The Market Explorer search field allows you to type in a domain and lists websites or articles similar to what you entered. Market Explorer also allows users to perform in-depth data analytics on These companies and markets.

SEMrush wins here because it has more tools dedicated to competitor analysis than Ahrefs. However, Ahrefs offers a lot of functionality in this area, too. It takes a combination of both tools to gain an advantage over your competition.

When it comes to keyword data research, you will become confused about which one to choose.

Both tools are great. Choose the one which meets your requirements and if you have any experience using either Ahrefs or SEMrush let me know in the comment section which works well for you.
