#9578. TOP 11 AI MARKETING TOOLS YOU SHOULD USE (Updated 2022)

If you’re late to the AI party, don’t worry. It’s easier than you think to start leveraging artificial intelligence tools in your marketing strategy. Here are 11 AI marketing tools every marketer should start using today.

Personalize is an AI-powered technology that helps you identify and produce highly targeted sales and marketing campaigns by tracking the products and services your contacts are most interested in at any given time. The platform uses an algorithm to identify each contact’s top three interests, which are updated in real-time based on recent site activity.

Seventh Sense provides behavioral analytics that helps you win attention in your customers’ overcrowded email inboxes. Choosing the best day and time to send an email is always a gamble. And while some days of the week generally get higher open rates than others, you’ll never be able to nail down a time that’s best for every customer. Seventh Sense eases your stress of having to figure out the perfect send-time and day for your email campaigns. The AI-based platform figures out the best timing and email frequency for each contact based on when they’re opening emails. The tool is primarily geared toward HubSpot and Marketo customers

Phrasee uses artificial intelligence to help you write more effective subject lines. With its AI-based Natural Language Generation system, Phrasee uses data-driven insights to generate millions of natural-sounding copy variants that match your brand voice. The model is end-to-end, meaning when you feed the results back to Phrasee, the prediction model rebuilds so it can continuously learn from your audience.

HubSpot Search Engine Optimization (SEO) is an integral tool for the Human Content team. It uses machine learning to determine how search engines understand and categorize your content. HubSpot SEO helps you improve your search engine rankings and outrank your competitors. Search engines reward websites that organize their content around core subjects, or topic clusters. HubSpot SEO helps you discover and rank for the topics that matter to your business and customers.

When you’re limited to testing two variables against each other at a time, it can take months to get the results you’re looking for. Evolv AI lets you test all your ideas at once. It uses advanced algorithms to identify the top-performing concepts, combine them with each other, and repeat the process to achieve the best site experience.

Acrolinx is a content alignment platform that helps brands scale and improves the quality of their content. It’s geared toward enterprises – its major customers include big brands like Google, Adobe, and Amazon - to help them scale their writing efforts. Instead of spending time chasing down and fixing typos in multiple places throughout an article or blog post, you can use Acrolinx to do it all right there in one place. You start by setting your preferences for style, grammar, tone of voice, and company-specific word usage. Then, Acrolinx checks and scores your existing content to find what’s working and suggest areas for improvement. The platform provides real-time guidance and suggestions to make writing better and strengthen weak pages.

MarketMuse uses an algorithm to help marketers build content strategies. The tool shows you where to target keywords to rank in specific topic categories, and recommends keywords you should go after if you want to own particular topics. It also identifies gaps and opportunities for new content and prioritizes them by their probable impact on your rankings. The algorithm compares your content with thousands of articles related to the same topic to uncover what’s missing from your site.

Copilot is a suite of tools that help eCommerce businesses maintain real-time communication with customers around the clock at every stage of the funnel. Promote products, recover shopping carts and send updates or reminders directly through Messenger.

Yotpo’s deep learning technology evaluates your customers’ product reviews to help you make better business decisions. It identifies key topics that customers mention related to your products—and their feelings toward them. The AI engine extracts relevant reviews from past buyers and presents them in smart displays to convert new shoppers. Yotpo also saves you time moderating reviews. The AI-powered moderation tool automatically assigns a score to each review and flags reviews with negative sentiment so you can focus on quality control instead of manually reviewing every post.

Albert is a self-learning software that automates the creation of marketing campaigns for your brand. It analyzes vast amounts of data to run optimized campaigns autonomously, allowing you to feed in your own creative content and target markets, and then use data from its database to determine key characteristics of a serious buyer. Albert identifies potential customers that match those traits, and runs trial campaigns on a small group of customers—with results refined by Albert himself—before launching it on a larger scale.

Albert plugs into your existing marketing technology stack, so you still have access to your accounts, ads, search, social media, and more. Albert maps tracking and attribution to your source of truth so you can determine which channels are driving your business.

There are many tools and companies out there that offer AI tools, but this is a small list of resources that we have found to be helpful. If you have any other suggestions, feel free to share them in the comments below this article. As marketing evolves at such a rapid pace, new marketing strategies will be invented that we haven't even dreamed of yet. But for now, this list should give you a good starting point on your way to implementing AI into your marketing mix.

#9575. What are flour enzymes?: Understanding a common flour ingredient.

If you look closely at a bag of King Arthur flour, you may see an unfamiliar ingredient listed there: enzyme.

We’re extremely thoughtful about every ingredient we use, across all King Arthur products and recipes. Our Food Philosophy guides every decision to ensure the quality of what we create, and that includes the enzymes in our flour.

Here’s exactly what flour enzymes are and why they’re included in flour.

Enzymes are found naturally in wheat, and thus are already present in flour. An enzyme is a protein produced by a living organism that acts as a catalyst to bring about a specific biochemical reaction.

The amount of enzymes in flour can vary based on growing conditions from harvest to harvest and year to year, so we add natural enzymes to correct for any variance and make sure our flour bakes more consistently — in other words, to make your baking even better. Those enzymes make up a very small portion of the total flour: less than 1%.

The enzyme we use in our flour is technically called fungal alpha-amylase. That’s a pretty technical name, so it is commonly labeled simply as “enzyme” on ingredient labels. “Alpha-amylase” is the actual enzyme, and “fungal” refers to the fact that the living organism that produces the enzyme is a fungus, not unlike yeast or a mushroom. Amylase may sound unfamiliar, but your body makes and uses it every day. When you eat, it begins breaking starch into smaller carbohydrates so you can draw on it for energy. Amylases added to flour perform a similar function.

Note: Though fungi are technically living organisms, enzymes are considered vegan, as they are not animal based.

Malted barley is an alternative source of enzymes that King Arthur has used in the past, but we found the efficacy can vary batch to batch. By swapping malted barley for straight enzymes, the flour produces more consistent results for our bakers.

Another reason we made the switch? Enzymes require less water and energy to produce than malt barley. As a Certified B Corporation, we're committed to being good stewards of our planet, so pivoting to a responsibly sourced ingredient with a smaller environmental footprint makes sense.

To put it simply, enzymes are added to flours to improve baking performance — they do not change the flour's nutritional value. More specifically, they help create the foods that feeds yeasts. The enzymes break down complex starches into simpler sugars; this, in turn, provides yeast with readily available fermentable sugar (food!), which enables yeast to work continuously and supports both fermentation and crust browning. This results in improved bread volume and crumb texture. Most other manufacturers of flour and yeasted mixes use enzymes for the very same reasons.

Ultimately, enzymes are yet another way for us to provide you with the most consistent flour — which means even better baking.

Cover photo and food styling by Liz Neily.

#9572. Make Your Burgers Juicier With One Creamy Ingredient (Hint: It's Not Butter Or Milk)

There are a million ways to make patties juicier, from mixing in grated butter to even marinating your burgers. But if you're looking for something a bit outside the box that doesn't complicate the recipe too much, stuffing the patties with Velveeta can give you some seriously cheesy, moisture-rich results.

While it may sound odd, this recipe is actually a variation of a Juicy Lucy cheeseburger, a Minnesota staple dating back to the 1950s. The idea is that by trapping Velveeta between two thin patties, the cheese melts into a liquid center that mingles with the rendered meat juices, adding moisture to every bite. If done correctly, the cheese should settle back into a gooey state while the patties rest, helping ensure that you don't burn your mouth on molten dairy on your first bite.

While you can always stuff your burgers with other cheeses, Velveeta has one major advantage. Thanks to its emulsifying and stabilizing agents, it's less likely to become greasy as it melts. Other meltable cheeses can release fat as they heat up, which isn't a problem when it can drip onto a grill but can create problems when you leave it no room to escape. Plus, the fact that Velveeta comes in blocks makes it extremely easy to shape to fit your patties, no matter how large or small you prefer them.

The classic Juicy Lucy burger may seem a little daunting, but the process is actually quite simple. Trapping the cheese between the patties and ensuring that all your ingredients and, more importantly, your grill are at the right temperatures are all you really need to worry about for something crisp, delicious, and juicy.

Starting with one part Velveeta to four parts beef is your best bet for this recipe. It's enough cheese to achieve that gooey center but not so much that it'll escape and ruin the integrity of your patties. It's also best to keep your patties flat rather than thick, which makes it much easier to pinch the seams and trap the Velveeta between them. Velveeta is easier to work with when cold, but keeping your beef cold is also a major benefit for your burger. Cold beef fat is less likely to smear and instead stays in little pockets that help keep the meat even juicier.

Grilling your burgers at the right temperature helps you achieve a good crust without excessive moisture loss, and it's doubly important when you stuff the patties. You want enough heat to char the exterior but not so much that the patties finish cooking before your Velveeta has the chance to melt. Around 400 degrees Fahrenheit is a good sweet spot. It may be useful to keep one side of your grill cool, letting indirect heat finish any patties whose exteriors have cooked too quickly.

#9569. Give Your McDonald's Egg McMuffin Double The Flavor With A Twist Workers Love

McDonald's Egg McMuffin is an iconic sandwich within the fast food breakfast realm. The chain took the McMuffin from good to great when its restaurants began toasting the English muffin halves in real butter rather than margarine. Customers have also found their own methods for upgrading this legendary breakfast sandwich, such as adding hash brown patties into the mix or giving it a flavor twist with sweet add-ons. The latter practice actually harks back to the 1970s, when the sandwich was served with sugary condiments like honey and jam. While that didn't last long as a standard practice, you can still DIY your own sweet toppings to get twice the eating pleasure out of just one Egg McMuffin.

Tristen Epps-Long, Season 22 winner of Bravo's "Top Chef" and a former McDonald's chef, shared this savory-sweet Mickey D's menu hack in an exclusive interview with Food Republic. "I like to take my sandwich apart a little bit, so half of it becomes jellied and buttered and the other half of it becomes open-faced and savory," the expert shared.

Executing this McMuffin double-down is easy to do. Simply remove the sandwich's top English muffin half, exposing the Canadian bacon, egg, and cheese below. This provides the open-faced, savory portion to enjoy — nothing more to do. On the other muffin slice, apply your choice of the Strawberry Preserves or Grape Jam commonly offered at McD's restaurants (or you can combine the two to give your spread a mixed berry vibe). Voila! You have something satisfyingly sweet to crown your McMuffin feasting.

When sweet meets salty, the resulting flavor wizardry is deeply satisfying. There are various other ways to apply this savory-sweet magic and take your McDonald's Egg McMuffin to the next level. Maple-flavored bacon is a popular breakfast staple, and you can bring that vibe to your McMuffin by pouring McDonald's Hotcake Syrup over the sandwich's Canadian bacon and letting it drip over the other elements. The maple-flavored sweetness brings a delightful dimension to the classic sandwich that is lip-smackingly scrumptious and the perfect foil for its salty heartiness.

Adding a packet of Mickey D's honey is another sweetening twist that gives your McMuffin honey ham flair. The honey is actually offered as a dipping sauce option for Chicken McNuggets, but no diehard Golden Arches diner will let that stop them from drizzling it onto a McMuffin for added sweetness.

McDonald's also frequently releases promotional, limited-time sauces, many of which hit those sweet-savory notes with aplomb. Options like Hot Honey Sauce and spicy-sweet Hunter Sauce were among limited-time options that dropped in 2026. You don't have to strictly wait for a limited-edition sauce, though — Mickey D's Sweet 'N Sour Sauce and Creamy Chili McCrispy Strip Dip are on offer year-round to lend sweetness and other flavor dimensions to your Egg McMuffin.

#9567. Heavy cream vs. whipping cream: What's the difference?: Understanding the right cream for your baking.

If you’re baking a recipe that calls for heavy cream, or picking up a carton to turn into whipped cream to finish a dessert, you may be confused when you hit the dairy aisle. There’s “heavy cream” — but also “heavy whipping cream” or, in some cases, just “whipping cream.”

So when it comes to heavy cream versus whipping cream, is there truly a difference?

Aside from being delicious, there are very specific definitions and standards that must be met in order for something to be labeled as heavy cream. It is made by separating the fatty top layer from the base milk layer during processing. The FDA states that heavy cream is cream that contains no less than 36% milk fat.  Comparatively, milk has 0% to around 3% milk fat, as well as a higher water concentration. Because of its fat content, heavy cream retains a rich taste and, when whipped, it excels at creating stiff peaks that hold their shape for a long time.

Whipping cream — sometimes called “heavy whipping cream” — is made using a similar process as heavy cream and is also the milk fat removed before milk is homogenized. However, whipping cream can contain somewhere between 30% and 35% milk fat content, according to FDA regulations. Because of its slightly lower fat content, it whips into a softer, more billowy cream, and it will deflate more quickly than whipped cream made with heavy cream.

Luckily, the difference in taste and performance between the two types of cream are not very discernible. This means you can use them interchangeably in recipes — and it's okay if you accidentally buy the "wrong" one. Both can yield a delicious bowl of homemade whipped cream. (Can’t justify buying a whole carton of either one? We’ve got you covered with an easy homemade heavy cream substitute.)

A note on King Arthur recipes: The King Arthur Test Kitchen prefers heavy cream in most instances, particularly when making whipped cream, because of the higher fat content. That said, you can substitute heavy whipping cream 1:1 in any King Arthur recipe that calls specifically for heavy cream without any issue.

As a general rule of thumb, use heavy cream for making stable whipped cream for topping pies, layered desserts like tiramisu or banana pudding, and any sweet where the structural integrity hinges on the cream really holding its shape. Heavy cream can also be handy for making cream scones and drop biscuits, where the richness of the dairy can shine through. For more heavy cream baking inspiration, check out these 12 recipes that call on heavy cream.

#9564. Not Butter, Oil, Or Lard: Chicken Skin Is 10x Crispier With This Rich Ingredient

Top-notch crispy chicken skin can steal the show. Sure, flavorful and juicy meat is tasty, but encased in a mouth-watering crispiness, the poultry experience only gets better. Achieving such a crackly bite entails light seasoning, low moisture, and – especially crucially – a good dose of rendered fat. Cooks often use butter, oil, or lard to improve crisping, but for an extra-rich rendition, reach for duck fat.

This under-utilized fat source is uber-savory, all while boasting a moderate smoke point. The ingredient comes as a firm paste at room temperature, meaning you'll need to melt the fat, then spread it onto the exterior of the chicken skin. The fat offers a two-for-one punch, adding both flavor and effectively crisping the skin as your chicken roasts.

It's a technique compatible with many poultry cuts. In addition to an entire bird, you can add a touch to skin-on thighs or breasts, enhancing the dish in more subtle ways. Or dive in all the way and even fry your chicken in duck fat. In addition to chicken, you could make duck confit, cooking the protein in its own fat. Duck fat gives skin-on poultry that extra oomph, crisping up the skin to a delicious effect.

Not sure what to pair with duck fat-covered chicken? The add-in meshes with various flavors. Season and bake a whole bird with salt and pepper alongside the fat, and you've already got a mouth-watering rendition as-is. The duck fat also pairs well with herbal seasonings like dried thyme and oregano, as well as a generous dose of garlic.

You could also consider then roasting the chicken on a bed of vegetables, letting the rich fat drip down and flavor alliums and root vegetables. Or cook the bird in the same vessel as potatoes, which can be tossed in more duck fat for good measure. Roast potatoes are 10 times richer with this magical fat; in combination with the crispy chicken skin, you'll get a truly decadent meal.

The abundant richness could use some bright elements to cut through the fat. Squeeze on some lemon — both during and after the cooking process — or finish with a drizzle of balsamic. A sprinkling of parsley goes a long way, as does a crisp glass of wine, making chicken skin a special occasion.

#9562. How to clean cast iron  : It’s simpler than you think.

Despite what you may have heard, cleaning and maintaining a cast iron skillet or Dutch oven isn’t difficult. It’s practically impossible to ruin a well-seasoned skillet, and despite your best efforts, sometimes food will stick. If your cast iron is covered in stuck-on bits of cheese from a batch of Crispy Cheesy Pan Pizza, here's how to clean it.

We can settle the debate once and for all: Yes, you can use soap to clean your cast iron. Dishwashing soap will not damage the seasoning that makes your skillet non-stick. Polymerized oil creates the layer of seasoning through heat, and dish soap isn’t strong enough to break that bond.

No, you cannot clean a cast iron skillet in the dishwasher. This will degrade the seasoning layer and cause it to rust.

You should not soak a cast iron pan either; the water will cause it to rust. If you do end up rusting your pan, you can still rescue it by scrubbing off the rust then re-seasoning the pan.

Using warm, soapy water, scrub the pan with a stiff-bristled brush or sponge to remove any food residue. Avoid harsh, abrasive scrubbers like steel wool or metal pads, which can strip the pan of its seasoning.

Once cleaned, fully dry the pan with a kitchen towel, or place it onto a burner over low heat so the water fully evaporates. Don’t walk away from the pan — it can quickly get smoky once the water has evaporated.

Regardless of which method you prefer, it’s imperative that the pan is fully dry. Water (not soap!) is the enemy of cast iron, which can cause it to rust. Once dry, add a few drops of neutral oil and spread all over the pan with a towel.

#9559. Give Leftover Mashed Potatoes A Caramelized, Crispy Side With A British-Style Classic

Not many dishes can compete with mashed potatoes. Beyond being the ultimate comfort food, and dare we say, the best preparation of potatoes, it's also super budget-friendly, and any leftovers can be saved and used up later. But let's face it: Nothing beats freshly cooked mashed tots. You could pop leftovers in the microwave or oven to reheat them, but they often come out dry and lackluster. To give them a new lease of life, borrow a tip from the Brits (who know a thing or two about mash) and fry them in butter instead.

Mashed potatoes fried in butter are part of an English comfort-food classic called bubble and squeak. The dish is traditionally made from Sunday roast leftovers, with mash and cooked cabbage or other veg shallow-fried in butter, lard, or meat drippings until a crispy brown crust forms. That crust is what brings the leftovers back to life, so it's essential to let it form. This comes down to the Maillard reaction, which occurs when amino acids in the potatoes react with reducing sugars. For that to happen, you only need two things: heat and time.

The potatoes need time to develop that crust. If you drop them into the pan and start stirring them around, they'll warm through, but they won't form a base layer. Instead, pat the mash into an even layer in the pan and cook it undisturbed over medium heat for around five minutes, or until the underside is deeply golden. Then flip it and repeat. You'll hear it sizzle and pop as it fries, which is said to be where the name bubble and squeak originates from.

In restaurants across the country, chefs are swapping high-end dining rooms for cozy neighborhood taverns – not to be confused with bars – serving food that's comforting, hearty, and nostalgic. Much of it looks like standard British pub grub, which makes bubble and squeak a natural fit for those looking to hop on the tavern food trend. It's a great side on its own, but with a few smart upgrades, it can easily become the main event.

Since the dish goes so well with butter, you can push it into true gourmet territory by whipping up a compound butter. For reference, this is softened butter mixed with sweet or savory flavorings. It truly couldn't be easier to make, yet delivers a world of flavor. In a nod to the dish's Sunday roast heritage, mix butter with garlic, chives, and horseradish, with a spoonful of English mustard for good measure. When it comes to frying, many chefs also advocate for using lard over butter since the semi-solid pork fat has a higher smoke point, allowing the mash to develop a crispier crust. For the best bubble and squeak, we'd recommend using lard to fry, then melting a knob of the compound butter over the finished dish.

Then there's what else can go into the dish. In the spirit of making use of your leftovers, toss in any spare roast meat, bacon, or sausage. Even better, cook the bacon or sausage from scratch in the pan first, remove it, add the butter, and let the potatoes soak up all that flavorful leftover fond. For a cheesy, tangy edge, mix a generous handful of grated cheddar and a spoonful of Dijon mustard into the mash before frying.

#9557. Grab A Box Of Cake Mix To Make A British-Style Dessert In Half The Time

Britain is home to some pretty controversial meals. There's the divisive beans on toast and the even more polarizing jellied eels. But one thing even the biggest haters can't fault Britain on is its dessert game, which is undeniably top-tier. There are countless cozy, comforting classics to choose from, like apple crumble, bread and butter pudding, and the elegant Victoria sponge. But one staple you can whip up using a boxed mix is a cake version of sticky toffee pudding.

Unapologetically indulgent, sticky toffee pudding has earned itself a spot in the British food hall of fame. But making it at home isn't as simple as making your typical sponge. Traditionally, the recipe starts with soaking and blending dates. After that comes the batter, the baking, and the toffee sauce, which all add up to a good couple of hours. If you fancy a quick fix, a boxed mix — we ranked popular brands from worst to best — gets you most of the way there in a fraction of the time, since the flour, sugar, and leavening agents are already pre-measured, taking the guesswork out of getting a reliably fluffy sponge.

The shortcuts don't stop there. To get that classic date flavor without the soaking and blending, swap in store-bought date paste instead. The dates are already crushed, so the paste can be stirred straight into the batter as the ultimate natural sweetener. The one thing a mix can't cover is the toffee sauce, but that's the easiest part anyway. Butter, brown sugar (ideally muscovado), and cream only need a few minutes of simmering to thicken and turn glossy, so you can whip it up while the cake bakes.

Sticky toffee pudding is a contender for Britain's favorite dessert and has a famous fan in Gordon Ramsay, who often serves it at his world-famous restaurants. But it's also the subject of a long-running debate that revolves around the dates. Recipes vary on whether the dates should be blended or simply soaked and stirred in chopped. Blended, they disappear seamlessly into the sponge, whereas chopped, they make their presence known with a chewy bite.

Fortunately, there's no right or wrong answer here, and if you enjoy more texture, you can swap the date paste for whole dates by pitting and roughly chopping them, soaking them in hot water (or coffee) until soft, then folding them into the batter just before it goes into the oven. The soaking softens the fruit so it turns jammy rather than leathery, and you can use some of the flavorful leftover liquid in place of part of the water the mix calls for.

Over in the U.K., sticky toffee pudding is often served with a scoop of ice cream, and the flavor is almost always vanilla. It gets popped on top of the warm, freshly baked sponge, where the hot and cold contrast adds a new layer to every bite. As it melts, it mingles with the toffee sauce to form a creamy, almost custardy pool that'll leave you licking your plate. You can experiment with other flavors, but there's no arguing that sweet, vanilla-forward ice cream is the perfect counterweight to the rich muscovado sugar and cooked-down toffee, cutting through the intensity so the pudding never turns cloying.

#9555. How to proof bread in the oven: Common challenge, simple solution.

During proofing, bread and other yeasted doughs do best in a temperature-controlled, humid, draft-free environment. Your kitchen counter may not cut it (especially in colder months), but is there a corner of your kitchen that fits that description? Yes, your oven — and you don’t even need to fire it up!

Yeast dough is happiest when rising at temperatures between 75°F and 78°F. It will certainly rise in cooler or warmer temperatures. But for most doughs, that range is optimum for both yeast development and bread flavor.

Your oven’s interior will pretty much mirror room temperature. And depending on the time of year (or how much you use air conditioning), that temperature could be pretty cool—too cool for yeast’s comfort.

To get the oven up to that ideal proofing temperature, people often turn to a couple of different methods. I decided to try a bunch of them to see which is best — and helpfully, there was a clear winner.

It’s tempting to simply preheat the oven for a minute or so to warm its interior; but not only is this hit-and-miss (How long should I leave it on? Will the oven get too hot?), it’s ineffective; the heat quickly dissipates once you turn the oven off.

Enter your oven light. When turned on, your oven light’s slow, gentle heat will gradually warm the oven to the desired temperature. After trying a number of different methods for proofing bread in the oven, including several listed below, this was my clear favorite because it created the ideal temperature (not too hot, not too cold), maintained that temperature for several hours, and was essentially failproof (no overshooting the temp, for example!).

It can take your oven a while to reach the desired temperature, especially if your kitchen is cold to begin with. With so many variables — season, climate, kitchen, oven — you’ll want to do a simple experiment to determine your own best method for turning your oven into an effective, efficient proof box:

Take your oven’s temperature before turning on the light. Then turn on the light and measure the temperature again at 15-minute intervals, to see just how quickly the light warms things up. For reference, the light in my electric oven takes about an hour to raise the oven’s interior temperature by 10 degrees, and another hour to raise it an additional five degrees; your results will probably vary a bit.

Warm your oven to about 80°F before turning off the light. Over the next couple of hours, the temperature will gradually drift down by about 10 degrees, giving your rising dough plenty of time in and around that 75°F to 78°F sweet spot.

Once you know how to warm your oven using only its lightbulb, think about maintaining humidity: Dry dough can develop a tough skin, which inhibits rising.

If you’re proofing dough in a bowl (or later, a shaped loaf in a pan), cover it with a clear plastic shower cap or reusable plastic bowl cover. Whatever you use, make sure it's large enough to form a “poof” on top, so the cover doesn’t touch the rising dough.

For shaped rolls (or anything else in a large, flat pan), use an extra-large shower cap; or simply drape the pan with well-greased plastic wrap, waxed paper, or parchment.

What if your oven doesn’t have a light, the lightbulb only lights when you open the oven door, or it’s a “cool” LED bulb?

Then your best bet is a pan of boiling water set on the lowest rack, which will both warm and humidify your oven’s interior. Place the bread dough on the oven’s middle rack; no need to cover it.  Set a shallow pan (e.g., 9" x 13" pan) on the lower rack, and add four cups of boiling water. Quickly close the oven door.

Your oven’s temperature will immediately rise by about 30 degrees, which will probably be warmer than you want. Cool it down by opening the door wide for about five minutes; the temperature should drop about 15 degrees.

As the water in the oven cools, the air around it cools, too. But it happens so gradually that your oven should still remain sufficiently warm for the one to two hours your bread typically needs to rise. For longer-rising breads, simply switch out the cool water with another pan of hot water, if necessary.

Some ovens actually have a proof setting or proofing drawer. I don’t always love using this setting, though: Most are programmed to temperatures ranging from 90°F to 100°F, far warmer than yeast dough’s optimal 75°F to 78°F. For best results, figure out how long it takes to reach about 80°F, then turn it off.

Tip #1: If you have to open the oven door to check your rising dough, don’t worry. Unlike the huge 15- to 20-degree drop you experience when opening a fully heated oven, the temperature inside your light- or steam-warmed oven will only drop by a degree or two.

Tip #2: Typically, you don’t preheat your oven with rising dough inside. So when your dough is close to fully risen, remove it from the oven and set it somewhere safe. (If there’s room, the top of your fridge is both warm and out of harm’s way.) Timed just right, your bread will be perfectly proved by the time the oven finishes preheating.

Tip #3: To prevent someone from killing your rising dough by turning on the oven (say, to warm their leftover pizza), write “NO!” on a sticky note and affix it to the oven’s start button. Really!

For the highly passionate bread baker (or a small baking business), an electronic proof box like the Brod & Taylor Proofer Pro is a step up from proofing dough in the oven. It controls temperature with exquisite precision, from cold-proofing (down to 41°F) for those overnight ferments up to 122°F for an express warmup, all while ensuring perfect humidity. Wi-Fi and programmable timers let you control your dough’s development for up to eight days. It’s literally set it and forget it — the process is simple, but the results are simply amazing.

Still looking for a warm, draft-free spot for your rising bread dough? Think beyond your oven to other major appliances: Both your clothes dryer and dishwasher can double as a proof box!

#9550. Not Mustard Or Mayo: Upgrade Your Ham Sandwich With One Rich Ingredient

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

A ham sandwich can be a pragmatic bite, assembled fridge-side during the late hours of the night. And yet with the right attention to detail, it's a template that readily turns luxurious, too. Take the jambon-beurre, for example — a Parisian sandwich enjoyed since the 19th century. The dish relies on classic French ingredients like baguette and jambon de Paris, a gently spiced wet ham. Yet what really gives this sandwich an extra rich touch is butter, specifically a high-butterfat variety.

Also called European butter, this extra-decadent style packs in up to 90% butterfat, significantly higher than the 80% composition popular in the USA. Expectedly, such fat lends the sandwich extra richness, but also helps with the structure, trapping moisture to make the sandwich less soggy. Anything fattier than the U.S. standard butter is an enhancement, but 85% butterfat is the ideal.

The benefits of using a rich butter aren't exclusively textural. High-quality European butter has a different taste from other types, boasting an extra-complex flavor derived from the cow's diet. It's often available cultured, slightly tart by way of fermentation. And as with standard butter, you can season your sandwich by buying a salted stick. Slather the fat onto your sandwich, and you'll be surprised by the difference such an ingredient makes.

A package of European-style butter is a worthy investment, even if you keep the other sandwich elements modest. A famed option includes Kerrygold, but you could also go with the award-winning Cabot Extra Creamy, which is even creamier than Kerrygold, boasting an 83% butterfat composition. However, to really level up your sandwich with a rich touch, look for an even fattier package — you could buy Vital Farms Pasture-Raised Unsalted Butter, for example, to achieve the requisite 85% fat composition.

Especially if you use only three ingredients like in a jambon beurre, it's such small details that make the difference. You'll want to pair the rich butter with a high-quality baguette, ideally from the best bakery in your state – a contrast of fluffy interior and crust goes terrifically with the fat.

And pay special attention to the ham you're using, too. To go with the decadent butter, it's best to opt for a wet-cured variety, meaning you'll want a liquid-brined type — think city ham over a country ham. Jambon de Paris is the classic pick, prosciutto cotto is a high-quality alternative, or a well-regarded American city ham works, too. Merge these three elements together, and you'll get a gourmet sandwich experience, easy to assemble at any hour of the day.

#9549. The secret to make-ahead pie crust? Pie crumbs.: Get ahead on your pie baking right now.

'Tis the season — to start thinking about holiday baking. And while this time of year is full of joy and celebration, it can also be stressful. We’re all searching for ways to get ahead of the curve, and one of the easiest? Make-ahead pie crust, made using pie crumbs.

I first learned of this technique from a 90-something friend with whom I love to talk baking. Over lunch one day, something she said about pie captured my attention.

"Did you ever hear of pie crumbs?" she asked. I admitted I hadn't — aside from the obvious: the scraps of pie crust left on the plate after the slice is gone. "My mother used to mix flour and salt and lard together to make this crumbly mixture that she'd store in a crock in the cellar. She called them her pie crumbs. When she wanted to make a pie, she'd just scoop out a few handfuls, add water, and roll out her crust."

Sounds like a good make-ahead solution for 100 years ago — but now that we have easy access to freezers, why not just make pie dough and freeze it in ready-to-roll disks? A couple of reasons, actually.

1) Pie crumbs allow you to make any amount of crust, from mini apple pies to a crust for a deep-dish 10" pie. With frozen disks, you're looking at a standard single crust — not always exactly what you want.

2) Pie crumbs save time. Remove however much of the crumbly mixture you need (more on this below) from the freezer, and within 15 minutes the fat is soft enough that you can add water and roll out your crust. Compare that to the hours it takes to thaw and roll a frozen disk of prepared crust — not to mention the elbow grease if your crust isn’t fully thawed.

3) Pie crumbs can be more stable in the freezer than pie crust disks. Why? Because without the added water, no ice crystals form. Ice crystals can damage the flour/water matrix, leading to changes in its structure (which can then potentially lead to changes in your pie crust).

Oh, and one other reason I like pie crumbs: If my friend's mother used them, they were probably a 19th-century kitchen time-saver. And I love the feeling of preserving and carrying forward our American baking traditions — even something as simple as a shortcut for pie crust.

Choose a standard pie crust recipe: Our Classic Double Pie Crust recipe is good choice, but anything that involves cutting fat into flour (lard, shortening, butter, etc.) will work.

Mix flour, salt, and shortening and/or butter: Follow your recipe up until all of the fat is incorporated into the flour. You should be left with a bowl of dry, crumbly dough that barely holds together when squeezed. If using butter, you should be able to see visible chunks scattered throughout the dough.

Weigh the pie crumbs: If you’re making a large batch of pie crumbs, it’s helpful to weigh and label the total gram amount so that you can easily remove the amount of pie crumbs for a single pie crust as needed. Our Classic Double Pie Crust makes 488 grams of pie crumbs; that means 244 grams per single pie crust. Label these amounts on your freezer storage bag.

Bag, label, and freeze the crumbs: Seal pie crumbs in an airtight, freezer-safe bag and place in the freezer, preferably in the back where it won't be subject to warm air wafting over it each time you open the freezer door.

Scoop crumbs out of the bag into a bowl: Whether one crust, two crusts, or one and a half, do the math and measure the crumbs based on your recorded gram amounts.

Let the crumbs thaw for 15 to 20 minutes or so: Wait until the butter chunks feel barely pliable in your fingers.

Add water and mix: Add water based on your original recipe amount, or just enough water to make a chunky mass when mixed. Squeeze and knead the dough briefly; all you're doing here is bringing the chunks together into one solid piece of dough.

Roll the dough, place in a pan, and bake accordingly: From here, your pie crust is the same as any fresh-made crust and can be filled and baked or prebaked for a no-bake filling. (Bonus: Because the crumbs were frozen and remain cold as you work with them, there's no need to chill your rolled-out crust before filling and/or baking.)

Fairly indefinitely, though the longer they're frozen, the more chance they have both to absorb freezer odors, and for the fats to start to go off. I've also found that, after about two weeks in the freezer, I need to add a touch more water than usual to bring the dough together — due to the drying effects inherent in freezing.

With pie season hard upon us, now's the time to try pie crumbs for make-ahead pie crust. Or maybe you have another old-fashioned pie trick up your sleeve? Share your favorite tips in the comments, below.

For detailed ingredient amounts for the crust demonstrated above, see our recipe for Classic Double Pie Crust.

And if you're looking for additional time-saving ways to use your freezer in the run-up to the holidays, check out our recipe for Homemade Brown and Serve Rolls and Apple Pie with Make-Ahead Filling.

#9547. Does Fluoride In Drinking Water Affect Intelligence? What The Evidence Reveals

Could childhood exposure to fluoridated water leave a lasting mark on cognition? Decades of data offer clues.

Could childhood exposure to fluoridated water leave a lasting mark on cognition? Decades of data offer clues.

Fluoride in community drinking water is not linked to lower adolescent IQ or poorer thinking skills later in life, a long-running US study finds.

Researchers followed a generation of Wisconsin school-leavers, examining cognitive performance from adolescence into their eighties.

Those exposed to fluoridated water did not show a consistent disadvantage compared with people whose communities had no fluoridation.

The findings address concerns that adding fluoride to drinking water to prevent tooth decay could undermine intellectual development.

Professor John Robert Warren, the study’s first author, said:

“Utah, Florida and many municipalities have chosen to remove fluoride from drinking water based on flawed studies that considered the IQ effects of exposure to massive doses of fluoride.

Because levels of fluoride added to municipal drinking water in the U.S. are so much lower, almost all prior evidence from those international studies is not relevant to U.S. public policy debates.”

The research draws on the Wisconsin Longitudinal Study, which began with over 10,000 people who graduated from high school in 1957.

Researchers combined school IQ records with historical information about community water fluoridation and naturally occurring fluoride levels.

Following participants into old age allowed researchers to examine whether childhood exposure was associated with lasting differences in cognitive performance.

Comparing communities requires care because their residents can differ in ways that also relate to cognitive performance.

Once those background differences were taken into account, there was no consistent evidence that exposure was associated with either better or worse performance.

The same broad pattern appeared when researchers focused on people who had lived in the same county since early childhood, increasing confidence in their estimates of exposure.

Overall, the findings suggest that growing up with fluoridated community water is not associated with poorer cognitive performance in old age.

The study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (Warren et al., 2026).

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean

#9545. Skip Boring White Bread: Make French Toast More Delicious With This Buttery Swap

If you were to think about sweet breakfast dishes, your mind would probably come up with French toast right alongside pancakes and waffles. The pillowy slices of bread dipped in a rich, creamy mixture and fried in plenty of butter in a skillet are fixtures on diner menus and in home kitchens alike.

A classic French toast recipe is typically made with white bread, which can soak up the combination of eggs, dairy, and sugar that makes up the custard base. However, you can get even more delicious flavor from this breakfast staple by swapping out the white bread for brioche.

Brioche is a French bread that has been around since at least the 15th century and is often associated with Marie Antoinette's purported declaration, "Let them eat cake." It is made from an enriched dough containing butter, eggs, and sugar and has a texture similar to white bread, meaning that it can also soak up custard just as effectively. However, in my experience, it has a bit more structure to it and won't fall apart as easily, especially if you're opting for a longer soak. Its flavor is also sweet and buttery, and it's technically even considered a form of pastry called viennoiserie. Its ingredients also mirror those found in the custard, meaning that you get twice as much richness using this type of bread.

It's worth noting that there are many brioche shapes out there, including small buns and even rings. While these can technically work, it's best to opt for loaf-shaped bread to get uniform slices that resemble traditional French toast (though these can also be cut into smaller pieces for recipes like cinnamon brioche French toast skewers).

Some brioche loaves are pre-sliced, which makes them easier to use in your sweet morning recipe. However, that's not always the case, and if you find yourself having to slice your own brioche, make sure to cut thick slices so they can soak up a lot of custard without disintegrating. Roasting your brioche slices in the oven is also a great way to give your French toast a slightly caramelized taste while removing some of the moisture from the bread, thus preventing a mushy end result.

There are also plenty of things you can do to the custard that will complement the flavor and texture of brioche. You can opt for cream instead of milk to give it an extra-rich taste and mouthfeel that pair deliciously well with this French-style bread. Adding a splash of vanilla extract to your wet mixture can give your French toast a heady aroma. Some liqueur can also give your recipe added dimension. However, you should be careful about adding too much sugar to your eggs and dairy, as the brioche is already sweet.

#9543. Evaporated vs. condensed milk: What's the difference? : Navigating the canned dairy aisle.

Navigating the dairy section at the grocery store is one thing, but when it comes to the canned stuff, how much do you know about the difference between evaporated milk and condensed milk?

Before we discuss what sets evaporated milk apart from condensed milk, it’s important to discuss their similarities. Evaporated milk and condensed milk are both concentrated liquids made from fresh milk that gets heat-treated until about 60% of the water content is removed. The primary difference between the two is the amount of sugar they contain and their resulting texture.

Evaporated milk will typically only contain lactose, or the naturally occurring sugars found in milk and dairy products. Condensed milk, on the other hand, contains around 40 to 45% added sugar. That contrast means condensed milk is much thicker (almost syrupy) and has a more pronounced sweet flavor (it’s no wonder it’s often referred to as sweetened condensed milk!), and evaporated milk runs watery in texture and is lighter in taste.

Because of the extreme differences in the sugar content and consistency, evaporated milk and condensed milk cannot be used interchangeably. There will be a very noticeable difference if you use evaporated milk in a recipe that was written to use condensed milk, or vice versa.

Using evaporated in a recipe that calls for condensed milk will result in a dessert that is too bland and watery, while using condensed milk in a recipe that calls for evaporated milk can make a dish way too sweet and thick. If your recipe calls for a very small amount (1 to 2 tablespoons) of condensed milk, you could get away with combining a spoonful of evaporated milk mixed with some sugar. But if your recipe needs one whole can of evaporated or condensed milk, be sure to use the correct type.

If you want to learn more about – and celebrate – the differences between evaporated and condensed milk, make this Tres Leches Cake, which is a fantastic recipe that utilizes the two milks with heavy cream in a luscious cake soak for dessert. For a different dose of double the milk, you’ll want to try this creamy, custardy Vanilla Bean Flan.

Evaporated milk provides richness and creaminess to dishes that are both sweet and savory. It’s often used to enrich custard-based pie fillings, like Hong Kong Egg Tarts, Delicata Squash Pie, and Pumpkin Pie. To round out your fall table and use up that can of evaporated milk, try the dairy ingredient in dinner recipes like Pumpkin Soup and Creamy Tomato Soup, or macaroni and cheese.

If you have an unopened can of condensed milk, you can also make dulce de leche with it. One way to go about it is to let it simmer in a pan filled with water for a few hours: Learn how to make it here.

#9542. 13 Sam's Club Bakery Items, Ranked Worst To Best

Sam's Club bakery solves the puzzle of how to get great baked goods at exceptional prices without having to hunt down a standalone bakery. The full-service department offers everything from sliced bread and rolls for everyday use to custom cakes for your most special occasions. Like the other items under the warehouse roof, the bakery stocks bulk quantities and super-sized versions of many of its best-loved bakes, giving your bank account a bit of a breather without requiring you to give up your appetite for the good stuff.

To get the best of the Sam's Club bakery, you'll want to know which picks are worth your money and which you can keep rolling right on past. I scooped up a selection of breads, rolls, and sugary delights to put under the microscope — my taste buds — and see how they rank amongst one another. Simple items like plain bagels shared the table with deluxe creations like caramel pecan banana loaf, all purchased at my Phoenix, Arizona-area Sam's locations. Prices and products shown are likely to vary based on region and warehouse. Clearly, membership has its privileges, but they're not all equally worth your money or your attention.

The double-baguette bag at Sam's Club was a qualified bargain at $2.98 at the time of purchase, though the bread inside is skinnier than a regular loaf. It's crusty and tender, perfect for breaking off chunks and dipping into olive oil or cheese dip. But it does limit your uses to silver dollar-sized slices, making mini garlic toast or bruschetta the most likely purposes. Slicing it lengthwise in longer sections will extend your toasting potential, but it's still a lot of bread to blow through before it starts to get even crustier on the counter.

Unless you have a house load of diners to feed, you may be getting more bread than you need, in a size and shape that makes using leftovers a bit limited. So while the bread itself is a wonderful version of a bakery-style baguette, the drawbacks of having two super-skinny loaves to work through may be reason enough to make a more suitable choice than this grocery store French bread.

There's no sense in raving over how good a plain bagel can be. They're plain for a reason: so they can hold all kinds of spreads and shmears and fillings without the taste of ramped-up bread getting in the way. But that doesn't mean every bakery gets the basic formula for plain bagels right. So having a bodacious bag of six overly large, unadorned bagels waiting at Sam's Club, among the fancier flavors, is a comfort to the purists of the bread-loving world. They do make an attractive haul at only $3.82 for six large pre-cut bagels, so there's that, at least.

I'm a fan of bagels, largely for the dense chewiness they offer, similar to a pretzel but with more potential for add-ons that don't fall off. I'd love to endorse these bagels more heartily, since they do their job perfectly well at a price that doesn't feel like you're being gouged. But in the end, they're just bagels, and Sam's has so many preferable baked goods waiting to be tossed in your cart.

Sam's Club is famous for its generous 12-inch pumpkin pies that appear at holiday time, priced at a seasonally considerate $5.98. But beyond the size and price, the warehouse bakery doesn't do much out of the ordinary with this bake. The crust is standard, the filling is customary, and the experience of digging into a slice is perfectly passable. In fact, if you're a dessert traditionalist, this will do nicely to replace anything you were planning on making yourself.

But the fact that the company mass-produces its pumpkin pies every year means you know exactly what you're getting here. If you keep your expectations in check and top it with a drizzle of chocolate or caramel sauce, plus some king-sized dollops of whipped cream, you can make it through another serving this year. Just don't count on it being anything more than average, even under all the decorations. You might even fare a little better with the comparable-yet-superior Costco pumpkin pie this year instead.

Something about the recipe Sam's Club bakery uses for its yeast dinner rolls makes them better than the thaw-and-bake versions I've become accustomed to. The chewy crust and soft centers of these baked spheres make them far too easy to snack on, which could readily deplete your stock for actual meals. The oversized bag comes with 24 rolls, so maybe you'll have enough for both if you can keep your appetite for bread snacks under control.

Maybe the best thing about these rolls is the price. You can drop $3.98 and end up with more bread than you can shake a stick at — a true magic trick in an economy that seems intent on crushing shoppers just hoping to come home with the basics. It'll put your imagination to the test when you realize your leftovers are crying out for creativity — cream puffs, mini-sandwiches, and bread pudding are all possibilities. Even if you freeze what you don't use for meals down the line, you'll be glad you made the purchase.

Similar to the yeast dinner rolls, Sam's Club bakery's brioche slider rolls are three-bite beauties that come pre-sliced to be filled with your favorite accouterments. But whether you opt to use them as dinner rolls or just toast them up and spread a little peanut butter inside instead of making actual sliders, they'll be just as satisfying. They have a buttery, eggy flavor that mimics full-sized brioche buns; the only thing reduced here is the scale, and even that makes them a fun choice for kid-size sandwiches of all sorts.

For $6.98, you get a generous stash of 24 slider buns. That may seem like too many, but if you use them in place of sliced bread for school lunches and work them into weekend meals, you'll blow through a whole bag before you know it. And if they're among your DIY barbecue spread or holiday celebration as cold cut holders, your guests are sure to gush over how cute and delicious they are.

Tangy, chewy, and ready to eat right out of the bag, the sliced sourdough loaves from Sam's Club bakery are a fantastic alternative to the rectangular bagged loaves the warehouse sells in its commercial bread aisle. It's the sort of sturdy bread that holds up well as grilled cheese sandwiches, Reubens without rye, and French toast, though you'll need to cut the slices in half for easier handling. And you can certainly cut it into strips to add to your grazing board for get-togethers or brunch sessions. It's the every-bread, and it's only $3.96 a loaf.

I tried to think of some drawbacks for this accommodating bake, but came up short. Despite having a host of sugary bites on the list that knocked my socks off, I thought this sourdough was excellent. It's pushed aside my usual go-to seedy whole-grain loaves to become my preferred full-size bread and an every-visit purchase.

Cocktail croissants, as Sam's Club calls them, are the bakery's sensibly sized version of the French classic, given all the love and attention of their continental counterparts, even in a warehouse grocery department setting. There's flakiness galore, thanks to an all-butter recipe that also comes through in the rich flavor. A carton of 20 croissants priced at $5.98, yet made with the same quality as their boulangerie counterparts, could be the bargain of our lifetimes.

The size is perfect for snacking, much better than the larger, sandwich-friendly croissants that cry out for fillings. Sure, you can break a bigger croissant into smaller pieces to make noshing a little more restrained. But when you can complete one in a few bites and walk away? That's sensibly sized croissant business. And if you're a fan of French pastries but cringe at spending big money to enjoy them, this first-rate batch of happiness is your golden opportunity, no splurging necessary.

Now this savage bake looks like the Ferrari of Sam's Club offerings, even before you take it out of the box. Through the cellophane window on top, you can see a heart-stopping coating of crumble in the perfect shade of toasted brown. The split in the top reveals a peek of golden pound cake. The overall effect is that you've stumbled onto the most gourmet banana bread you've ever encountered — right across from the bulk fabric softener and double-paned window vendors.

The chewy crust is just shy of decadence, feeling more like an old-fashioned homemade crumble top without the oats. The banana bread beneath is equal parts sweet loaf and pound cake, capturing the cozy vibe but with a stroke of elegance that elevates it. I would eat this in all forms: cold out of the freezer, room temperature straight out of the box, or warmed up with a scoop of ice cream on the side. There's no situation that this fantastic loaf can't handle.

Gourmet bakeries have nothing on the patisserie spirit of Sam's Club mini creme pies. These refrigerated bakes shrink the lush goodness of full-sized pies into a six-pack of petite pastries, two each of chocolate creme, peanut butter chocolate, and cherry cheese pie. The reduced scale doesn't diminish the delicious returns; there's bold flavor and silky texture that make even a single slice a luxurious moment.

Though all of these pies are a real treat, there's a definite hierarchy to their enjoyability. The cherry cheese pie is a mellow bite that resurrects the vintage pie flavor from long-ago Sunday dinner desserts, while the chocolate creme reminds me of a dessert-style specialty. But the top spot belongs to the peanut butter chocolate pie, which calls to mind luxury cheesecakes made by maestros of the baking world. It's a sweet dream of a Sam's Club baked goodie, and at $10.98 for six, it's one that doesn't require reservations — of any kind.

Any Sam's Club shopper will tell you that the bakery muffins are a cake situation, not a muffin scenario. These super-sweet, super-sized bakes are too big and too delicious to qualify as traditional muffins, and when the warehouse puts a holiday spin on the usual recipes, that dessert-ready razzmatazz doubles up. They're the domed bakery-style muffins too, so they look extra grand on your snacking spread.

I've had the store's traditional chocolate, blueberry, and banana nut muffins enough to be inured to their charms by now. But slicing into these three upgraded flavors was a seasonal revelation I won't soon get over. The red velvet is the best of the bunch, tasting like a pricey chef-inspired creation, while the pumpkin spice takes a more measured approach than the usual fall-flavored treats. And the butter pecan is a study in subtlety, with just the right balance of sweet and earthy notes. These should be year-round items.

Another refrigerated item due to the meltable toppings and delicate frosting, the gourmet cupcake eight-pack at Sam's Club bakery is a fancier take on the workaday cupcakes that come in a set of 30, and all taste exactly the same. In this package, you get a variety of chocolate, strawberry, and Meyer lemon, all wearing the frills and finery you'd find in a much pricier cupcake at a specialty shop. The $12.97 price tag that splits into $1.62 per cake assures you that you can have nice things without having to cash in your IRA.

Even if you choose to crack open your piggy bank for these, you'll be getting more than your money's worth. The chocolate cupcake is exceptional, lush, and over-packed with fudgy goodness thanks to a generous heap of ganache frosting. The strawberry is well-balanced, with its own floral ganache whip, and the Meyer lemon, with a dollop of gelee in the center, is bright as sunshine, authentic-tasting. There's a moist crumb and silky frosting in every cake, too. They're a little too complex to pass off as a home bake, but these are top-tier bakes that make a perfect meal finisher at a dinner party or a lovely surprise for birthday revelers.

I'm a frequent Sam's Club shopper, so I had some idea of which items I thought would be worth including. But with items changing so often and seasonal picks popping up throughout the year, I also grabbed some new selections to give my list a bit of variety. Even familiar items like bagels and baguettes took on a different status when compared to novelties like specialty banana bread and gourmet brownies.

To taste test everything fairly, I used my standard method: the one-bite sample. I gauged freshness and texture as well as taste to arrive at an all-encompassing enjoyability factor for each item. Anything that was deemed worthy of a second or third bite became an obvious high-ranking find, while the items that were less captivating sank to the bottom. The standard-issue picks that were neither dazzling nor disappointing fell somewhere in the middle of the list.

#9538. Upgrade Your Wendy's Baked Potato With This Delicious, High-Protein Ordering Request

Wendy's sells two sides you simply cannot find at McDonald's or Burger King: cups of chili (which you can easily turn into a game-day nacho dip) and its famous baked potatoes. Long past when other fast food empires might have chucked the baked potato as a nuisance menu item, Wendy's continues the tradition of serving up convection-cooked spuds, as it has done for over 40 years. Now, if a baked potato sounds grand right about now, but you have a daily protein goal you need to meet, you're in luck. While the potato itself actually puts up decent numbers, with 7 grams of protein, adding a double portion of chicken to it will put the protein content basically through the roof.

The grilled chicken has about 19 grams of protein per serving, so with a double portion, plus the baked potato, you're getting a whopping 45 grams of the essential macronutrient in one sitting. When the average 200-pound man requires 72 grams of protein, that's over half the suggested amount needed in just one meal (and if you're worried about getting too much protein, you could just order one serving of chicken to put on your baked potato).

Unfortunately, short of ordering two salads and a baked potato, this spud boost simply cannot be obtained through digital means. Instead, you'll have to walk up to the counter, or drive to the drive-thru speaker, and place the order in person. Is that a little extra work? Maybe, but the protein bump is worth it.

We have to be honest; the idea of eating a plain baked potato and two portions of grilled chicken, as-is, isn't the most appetizing or flavorful meal to cross our minds. However, there are plenty of additional ingredients that you can order while you're at Wendy's to help make it a bit more palatable (and one of them will add significantly more protein to the dish). For example, if you wanted to keep the core elements the same with just one additional ingredient, you could drizzle on any of Wendy's sauces; we're partial to the idea of Creamy Ranch or Honey Mustard for this application, but if you like a little heat, go ahead and use the Scorchin' Hot.

If your stomach can handle the dairy, you might double up by requesting the sour cream, and also ask for a side of nacho cheese sauce, to give the baked potato not just a tender chicken topping, but a creamy, luscious element, too (if you like your cheese on the stronger side, too, Wendy's carries blue cheese crumbles as well as plain old shredded cheddar). Heck, add bacon crumbles to the meal. Finally, you simply cannot forget the iconic baked potato and chili pairing. When added to the spud and the chicken, the whole meal comes to 64 grams of protein because the chili contains an extra 19 grams.

#9534. Not Chicken Or Beef: Give Canned Soup A Major Protein Boost With One Frozen Ingredient

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

When you're not in the mood to cook, a decent can of hearty soup from the pantry can be quite satisfying. And when you're feeling under the weather, even a thin broth can do wonders for your constitution. Some of the off-the-shelf stuff is better than others, but there are plenty of ways to upgrade your canned soup and get it darn near homemade. And if you want a boost of flavor, texture, and protein with hardly any extra work, you can achieve it with one simple supplemental component: Try adding frozen dumplings to your canned soup for an incredible transformation that will transport you from plain ol' shelf-stable stock or stew to a delicious, substantial meal that can take on takeout any day of the week.

Using frozen dumplings in your canned soup allows you to tweak the recipe to bring more nuance to what's behind the tin, creating a new and fresh blend of flavors that you just can't get straight from a can. It's sort of like frozen vegetables versus canned. Even though they are generally blanched before freezing, frozen vegetables often taste fresher because they aren't subjected to high heat for long periods of time, as are their canned counterparts. Frozen dumplings come pre-cooked, but they are flash-frozen at very low temperatures to maintain their flavor and textural integrity. Dumplings will add a bit of toothsome chew to your soup and a nice hit of protein.

When you're thinking dumplings, your mind may go directly to Asia, but there are Polish pierogi, Russian pelmeni, and, heck, even frozen ravioli or tortellini work for our needs, some with more protein than others. For example, Mrs. T's Four Cheese Medley Pierogies have 7 grams of protein per serving; Bibigo Beef Pho Flavor Soup Dumplings come in at 11 grams; and there are plenty of frozen dumpling options at Trader Joe's, ranging from about 7 to 16 grams of protein per serving.

You can match your dumpling with your soup. Milder fillings, like shrimp, often go better with thinner broths, so the interior flavor doesn't get lost. Pork and chive fillings, on the other hand, can stand up to bolder flavors and work well with rich stews. When working with a dairy-based soup, like cream of chicken or cream of broccoli, you might want to try some cheesy pierogi. And if you want to bulk up your canned soup and don't need the protein, frozen gnocchi goes with just about anything.

If you're using varieties that are usually boiled or steamed, you can make it super easy and just add them directly into your soup, frozen, but they'll need some extra time simmering to fully heat through. Or cook them partially, then add them to the soup as it heats up. When working with a particularly thin-skinned style, like certain gyoza, you may want to fry them up crispy first to fortify the exterior.
