#9520. 6 Once-Popular Buffet Chains That Went Extinct

All-you-can-eat buffets were once a common feature in the restaurant world. Now-defunct chains like Shoney's, Fire Mountain, and Luby's were popular because the businesses offered endless plates of a wide variety of foods for a set price. This allowed customers to try new things and enjoy familiar items without having to order separate dishes and paying more. The concept was so popular even fast food chains, like Popeyes, had buffets. But the format is becoming a rarity these days, partially due to rising food and labor costs.

There are still a few all-you-can-eat buffets around. For instance, seafood buffets are popular on the East Coast, as well as in Las Vegas. And mega-retailer Walmart was able to help revive the failing Mr. Gatti's Pizza, which was once known for it's oversized buffets. But today, the pizza restaurant is much smaller and operates a more traditional order-and-take-out model. Not every chain was as lucky as Mr. Gatti's, and that's why this list highlights some of the reasons once-popular buffet chains don't exist anymore.

Souplantation, which was called Sweet Tomatoes outside of its home state of California, was a self-service buffet that operated over 120 locations in the mid-2010s. The restaurant first opened in 1978 and was known for its large selection of soups and fresh muffins. Even though the chain was popular, it began to falter as the minimum wage and rent prices increased. These combined factors led to the company filing for bankruptcy in 2016.

The business was already on shaky ground when the COVID-19 pandemic hit in 2020. Because of the uncertain nature of the disease early in the shutdown, self-service wasn't allowed in restaurants. Souplantation couldn't last without customers any more than it could suddenly become a full-service eatery. So, in May 2020, the last 97 locations were permanently shut down.

But that wasn't the end for the brand, because there are now two re-opened Sweet Tomatoes restaurants. One is in Arizona, and the other is in Florida. That might make the company more of a novelty for now than a comeback success story, with a third location set to open in California in 2027, there's no telling what lies ahead for the brand.

Old Country Buffet was one of the largest buffet chains in the country, with nearly 400 stores during the early 2000s. It was known for its selection of over 90 items that were made from scratch each day. It was so popular it was able to grow to 200 locations in just a decade and rivaled Outback Steakhouse in sales. This beloved buffet closed during the COVID-19 pandemic, but financial issues had plagued the business long before.

It began in 2006, when the brand's parent company, Buffets, Inc., merged with Ryan's. The move gave the company more buffet concepts and locations, but it also brought massive debt. That caused the business to file for bankruptcy protection in 2008 and again in 2012. Old Country Buffet's parent company was bought by Ovation Brands Inc. (also called Buffets LLC) in 2015, but the new owners shuttered almost 100 stores early the next year.

There was another bankruptcy in 2016, which further weakened the brand. When the COVID-19 pandemic hit a few years later, the loss of its remaining customers sealed the chain's fate. A final Chapter 11 protection was filed in 2021, which closed the remaining stores.

HomeTown Buffet was never as widespread as its sister restaurants, Old Country Buffet and Ryan's, but at its height there were over 120 locations throughout the U.S. The company was started in 1989 and, as the name implies, was dedicated to home-style cooking and comforting foods. The brand became part of Buffets, Inc. in the mid-1990s. But not long after, HomeTown Buffet's parent company began having legal and financial troubles due to alleged fraud and multiple bankruptcies.

The first bankruptcy happened in 2008, and it did help reduce some of the debt the company had. But it wasn't enough to keep the business going. So, other bankruptcies were filed in 2012 and 2016. More than 70 locations were closed with the Chapter 11 protection in 2016, which was over half of the brand's stores.

There were legal issues, too, with a 2010 lawsuit alleging several of the parent company's executives had used nearly $40 million as their personal funds. In 2015, the brand settled a class action filing alleging it hadn't paid workers their final wages for around $2 million. There was even an investigation by the State of California in 2016 over whether the company had illegally laid off workers without the required warnings. In the end, all of the problems HomeTown Buffet had led to one final bankruptcy filing in 2021, which closed all the remaining locations.

Those who were lucky enough to eat at a Ryan's Buffet when the chain was open are likely to remember the famous yeast rolls. The bread and honey butter it was served with were key parts of this buffet experience at any of the restaurant's over 350 locations during its height. But the business was also owned by the parent company of HomeTown and Old Country Buffets, so Ryan's suffered from the same financial mismanagement and legal troubles the other businesses did.

The issues started in 2006 when Buffets, Inc. wanted to buy Ryan's. Shareholders at the time were unhappy the company had been put up for sale without full transparency, so they filed a lawsuit to stop the sale. Ryan's settled with the shareholders and went ahead with the merger. But that led to large amounts of debt.

In 2008 and 2012, the company began filing bankruptcies, which led to a domino effect of locations closing, beginning in 2016. The COVID-19 pandemic didn't help the business any more than its parent company being accused of mishandling over $4 million in Paycheck Protection Program funds did. One final bankruptcy finished off the chain in 2021.

Founded in Pensacola, Florida in 1991, Barnhill's Buffet was known for Southern-style food that the founder, Steve Barnhill, was proud to say was better seasoned than other all-you-can-eat options. That superior taste helped expand the brand to over 40 locations across six states by 2005. However, the food alone couldn't keep the doors open.

Several locations in Southern Mississippi were heavily damaged by Hurricane Katrina in 2005, causing them to close. That was just the start of Barnhill's financial troubles. The company filed for bankruptcy in December 2007, while nearly $28 million in debt. Sixteen stores were sold to Star Buffet Management Inc. in 2008, but just a few years later multiple locations were shuttered. Barnhill's had just one location left after closing the rest in the early 2000s. The Jonesboro, Arkansas store held on until 2021 but was forced to close due to owing a substantial amount in back rent.

While that was the end of the original brand, Steve Barnhill created another restaurant bearing his name called Barnhill's Steaks & Buffet. This stand-alone eatery is found in Jacksonville, Arkansas, and even though it isn't as cheap as the very first all-you-can-eat buffet, the prices are shockingly low.

Whether you knew it as Furr's Cafeteria or Furr's Fresh Buffet, this business was a powerhouse of cafeteria and buffet-style dining from its founding in the 1940s until it was shuttered in early 2021. The all-you-can-eat concept boasted nine buffet stations for everything from ice cream to salads to a variety of proteins and operated in five different states. But things weren't going smoothly for the brand after it reformatted its cafeteria locations into buffets.

As early as 2008, Furr's was having financial troubles and was reportedly more than $40 million in debt. An ice storm in 2013 further weakened the business when numerous customers in Texas and Oklahoma weren't able to dine out, leading the company to declare its third bankruptcy in 2014. Locations began closing, with one Midland, Texas store going out of business in 2018.

Just a few years later, the chain's parent company, Fresh Acquisitions LLC, declared bankruptcy again, after it was accused of mishandling millions of dollars of Paycheck Protection Program loans. #9512. The best Thanksgiving baking tips from Ina Garten, Erin McDowell, and more pro bakers: Top tips from the Things Bakers Know podcast.

It’s the most wonderful baking season of the year, and to help you bake your best, we have top tips from some of the country’s best bakers, pulled from conversations on the Things Bakers Know podcast. Below, you’ll find Thanksgiving strategies from podcast guests Ina Garten, King Arthur’s Martin Philip, Erin McDowell, Helen Goh, and many more of our baking friends.

“The one thing I think people think they can do is multiply a recipe times four and think it’s going to come out fine, which it won’t,” Ina shared on her podcast episode. Instead of taking one recipe and just multiplying by three or four, she suggests either baking the original recipe multiple times, or doubling it and baking two or three times, depending on how many people you’re feeding. Just don’t multiply more than once! If you do, the leavening and flavoring starts to get thrown off.

If you’re baking for a lot of people, Ina also suggests making recipes scaled for a baking sheet. As she explains, “It’s easier to bake, and it’s easier to cut.” We’d recommend Slab Chocolate Pecan Pie, Pumpkin Cake Bars with Cream Cheese Frosting, or Walnut and Oat Slab Pie.

While you may be excited to try out a show-stopping recipe from a brand-new cookbook, Ina recommends resisting temptation. “You don’t want to test something you haven’t made a million times,” she cautions. “Even for me, it adds enormous stress.” Instead of turning to a first-time recipe, Ina highly recommends that you “do the things you know will come out perfectly every time.” And if you do want to make a new-to-you recipe this Thanksgiving, consider baking it once or twice in the weeks leading up to the holiday, so you have the chance to practice and work out any kinks (like figuring out make-ahead components or fridge storage) before hosting on the big day.

No one wants a soggy bottom on their pie, especially a super-juicy one like apple pie. Erin McDowell has lots of tips to avoid a soggy bottom, but her biggest one is to precook your apple filling before assembling your pie. “We can't necessarily predict how juicy any given fruit is, so even if you're using the same apple … each time, they are going to be a little bit different,” she explained on our podcast episode all about apples. Precooking the filling allows you to adjust based on the juiciness of the fruit you’re using that day. “If you're dealing with not-very-juicy apples, you may not have to cook it as long. If they're really juicy, you may have to cook it longer, but the process is the same.”

Pie crust can be incredibly intimidating for some bakers. But pie queen Stacey Mei Yan Fong says the key to success is sometimes to chill out, figuratively and literally. “The best thing you can do is just chill, as in calm down. You're not doing brain surgery,” she reminded Jessica in our Thanksgiving pie episode. “And also use your fridge!” As she points out, “the minute things start getting too wet or things start getting too warm, that's when people panic.” So take a moment to chill the dough and make it easier to work with. If the butter's getting soft or your pie dough is getting difficult to work with, just put it in the fridge to cool down for 10 to 15 minutes.

It’s not just the fridge, either — your freezer can also be incredibly helpful. Stacey likes to freeze her pies before baking, which she says helps the crimping hold its shape as it bakes. And remember that, as Stacey points out, “Pie is kind of a lesson in patience.”

On our special Holiday Q+A Extravaganza, King Arthur’s Director of Baking Education Amber Eisler has a crucial tip for avoiding runny apple pies — make sure you see your pie filling actively bubbling through the vents in your pie crust. As she explains, “It means the filling has boiled and bubbled, so the starches in the filling are actually thickening, which is a super important part of [avoiding a soupy pie].”

There’s a lot of cooking and baking happening around Thanksgiving, which means your oven can get pretty crowded, pretty quickly. But be wary of overfilling it. Even though your oven may have up to three racks inside, Martin Philip cautions against using them all at the same time. “Don’t make the mistake of crowding the oven when it comes to rolls. Let bread have its moment,” he says. Bake your pies the day before to save oven space; a turkey, too will stay hot out of the oven for hours. When baking rolls, you want “top and bottom heat, use your convection setting, make sure that air is moving,” says Martin. “Guard the rolls, y’all!”

Cookbook author and professional psychologist Helen Goh believes in the power of baking to bring meaning and fulfillment to our lives. During this busy holiday season, full of messy kitchens, family squabbles, lengthy to-do lists, and lots of hosting, it can be easy to get overwhelmed. But baking can actually be a calming, comforting activity right now. “Some people say baking makes them nervous because you have to focus,” says Helen. But part of the therapeutic effect of baking comes from forcing us to focus on a single task at hand. As she points out, “that takes you away from all that white noise about what you did yesterday or what's going to happen tomorrow,” and instead allows you to live mindfully in the moment.

Happy Thanksgiving from all of us here at King Arthur. If you run into baking troubles or just need a little support in the kitchen, our Baker’s Hotline is here to help.

#9511. For Softer French Toast, Grab This Classic Spiced Dessert (Goodbye, White Bread)

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

For a wonderfully decadent brunch-style meal at home, you can go with a classic Eggs Benedict or a tasty rosemary and olive frittata, but it can be hard to get hollandaise sauce just right, and the frittata requires a lot of prep and time in the oven. A quick French toast, on the other hand, is simple and can be ready to hit a hot pan in only a few minutes. You just have to whisk your ingredients, soak the bread, and cook it until it's gently browned. If you want to go out of the ordinary, there are some amazing upgrades you can make to your custard-dipped bread, like a stuffed fried sandwich with peanut butter and jelly. But to up the earthy sweetness with a delicious, distinctive flavor, you should try pumpkin bread French toast.

Using pumpkin bread for the base of your French toast will bring rich, slightly vegetal, natural-tasting sweet notes, with a backbone of deep, warm, baking spices. It's bold and full-bodied without being too heavy or cloying on the palate. Once you have the bread, it doesn't require any extra preparation outside the standard French toast. It will cook up crispy on the exterior, with a nice caramelization, and remain soft and moist on the interior, but still airy, without getting soggy and overly weighed down by your egg and dairy mix. It's the perfect weekend indulgence for some cozy time with the family or a quick and easy treat for yourself.

Start with any simple pumpkin bread recipe. It's best to make it ahead of time, generally at least a day or so before, so it will be completely cooled, rather than hot out of the oven (and thus likely to fall apart). For the custard (or batter), you can use the standard formula of eggs, milk, vanilla extract, and ground cinnamon — or add cardamom, allspice, and a pinch of brown sugar for more flavor and caramelization. You'll want your bread slices half an inch to an inch thick — too thin, and they'll dry out in the pan; too thick, and they won't heat through completely without the exterior burning.

Most basic pumpkin breads are spiced with cinnamon, nutmeg, and clove, but you can spread your wings a little with ginger and anise for an aromatic kick of spice, salt to highlight the other seasonings, or molasses for some robust, rustic undertones. And for a big pop of flavor, try a bit of Chinese five-spice powder, a blend of cinnamon, fennel seeds, clove, star anise, and Sichuan pepper that will really wake up your taste buds. Pumpkin bread with chopped nuts or chocolate chips also works beautifully for French toast.

You can even make your bread weeks ahead of time and store it in the freezer, covered in plastic wrap and aluminum foil, or prep individual slices and freeze them in plastic, separated with parchment paper inside an airtight container. Just be sure to thaw them so that they don't go into your egg mix completely frozen. And when the French toast is cooked and it's time for plating, you can take the pumpkin theme to the next level with some shelled pumpkin seeds (pepitas) on top for a festive touch of crunch.

#9510. What Does Gen Z Think About Political Polarization?

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

Polarization is a fact of political life in the U.S. today. Gen Z, however, is less inclined than older generations to view it as a permanent fixture in American politics, according to research by students in the Stanford political science course Democracy in the Balance: Polarization and the Road Ahead. Students found that Gen Z is more optimistic than any other age group about the possibility of bridging the political divide in America.

“Polarization doesn’t seem to be a fixed trend in Gen Z’s minds,” said Jadon Urogdy. “We have a bright future. Our identities and views are still malleable, and that’s exactly why this moment matters so much.”

Urogdy and his classmates also found that Gen Z, which is the cohort born between 1997 and 2012 and considered the first true “digital natives,” is more comfortable than their elders in having a political conversation online—findings that suggest they may be more reachable and receptive to online interventions aimed at reducing polarization.

Urogdy’s results were among many findings from Democracy in the Balance: Polarization and the Road Ahead, a spring quarter course taught by Ashley Fabrizio, a Stanford alum and head of research at the nonpartisan think tank More in Common. Working with Fabrizio and her team, students created and conducted a nationally representative survey of 1,610 U.S. adults that oversampled Gen Z to provide a more granular look into their political attitudes and opinions.

Fabrizio, who has taught the course for three years, has found that working with students surfaces concerns that standard polling may miss. “If we want to know what Gen Z’s political beliefs and attitudes are, we should let our students, as members of Gen Z, use their intuition to decide what matters in a survey,” Fabrizio explained.

Working in small groups, students were allocated several minutes of survey time to explore topics such as the political influence of online content promoting masculinity—aka the “manosphere”—the religious revival in Gen Z’s lives, and their beliefs about the American dream. Fabrizio guided students step by step through survey design, showing them how to craft research questions, field the survey, analyze data, and, finally, present their findings.

Students also examined the academic literature on polarization’s effects in American politics, such as how it contributes to political gridlock, drives support for political violence, and erodes trust in American institutions.

“There are many legitimate divisions in politics over competing policies and values, but polarization often drives us apart unnecessarily,” said Fabrizio. “Young Americans will have to find their own ways of bridging partisan differences and overcoming misconceptions about one another. I hope this class helps students see the value of doing so and gives them a sense of agency in addressing polarization.”

Natalia Galperin was excited about the opportunity to run her own study from start to finish, a first for the Stanford undergrad majoring in psychology. She also wanted to expand on her prior work as a research assistant for political scientist Shanto Iyengar in his Political Communication Lab, where she studied the effects of negative political campaign ads.

For her research project, Galperin examined the role of social media in inflating Gen Z’s hostility toward people from the opposing political party, a phenomenon political scientists call “affective polarization.”

“We thought Gen Z would be more polarized and misinformed because we get so much of our news on social media compared to older generations,” Galperin said.

What she and her classmates found reveals a more complicated picture.

While Gen Z respondents who said they used social media daily or almost daily were more likely to dislike the opposing party, their scores were almost identical to those of other generations.

“We found that greater social media engagement is generally linked to more polarized views of political parties, and the effect is seen at similar rates across all generations, not just Gen Z,” said Galperin, who will be interning with More In Common this summer.

Practices to help campus communities connect across lines of race, faith, ideology, and more.

Galperin also wanted to know whether social media deepens the divide between what Gen Z thinks people from the other side believe versus what they actually think, a phenomenon known as “perception gaps.” In testing people’s perceptions on immigration, she found that Gen Z did not appear to hold wildly distorted views about the other side—findings that push back against the familiar narrative that being online warps a person’s perceptions of politics.

Taken together, actively using social media seems to harden Gen Z’s feelings more than it distorts basic facts.

The class also found a wide range of political viewpoints, including differences between Gen Z who identified as Democrats and Republicans.

For example, in Urogdy’s project, he and his teammates found that those who were the most confident that polarization can be reduced identified as conservatives and Republicans, while liberals and Democrats believed the opposite—a finding that Urogdy said tracks with prior research: A person’s view of government depends on whether or not their political party is in control.

Galperin’s team also found lower levels of affective polarization among Republicans and Gen Z overall, and Democrats who reported actively using social media daily have higher perception gaps on immigration-related issues than average.

Another student team’s project revealed further complexities. They found that many Gen Z respondents are more likely than other generations to attribute problems like the affordability crisis to systemic failures in democracy itself rather than to specific policies or leaders. In their data, a notable share of young people said the system itself “is not capable of doing its job,” signaling a deeper, structural disillusionment.

“I think we’re all exhausted by the political system,” Urogdy said. “There’s this underlying feeling that what we want isn’t being translated into tangible change, and I think that there’s this overall feeling that instead of having animosity towards people across the aisle, there’s an animosity towards the system itself.”

Urogdy is pragmatic about what comes next.

“We can’t say polarization will disappear if we will it away,” said Urogdy, who is majoring in political science. Now, he feels he has a better understanding of what kinds of solutions matter. If people are disillusioned with the system, surface-level fixes—such as messaging—won’t last, he said. Efforts need to be ongoing. “If Gen Z is still one of the most reachable generations, the answer is sustained civic engagement, where we can rebuild trust in the system while working to reform it. We have a long path ahead,” said Urogdy, who said he is optimistic.

Fabrizio, too, is hopeful. “Gen Z is inheriting a polarized nation, but they are inheriting deep wells of democratic vitality, as well,” Fabrizio said. “America has a long history of self-government, a robust civil society, and communities that remain deeply committed to democratic values. Gen Z has high standards for our democracy, but living up to them is within reach. I hope older generations will listen and be inspired by Gen Z’s vision for the American dream.”

#9509. How to turn any bread dough into rolls: Transform your favorite bread loaf into shareable rolls.

So you have a beloved bread recipe that you'd like to turn into fluffy, single-serving rolls, but you don’t know where to start. We’re here to help — let’s get rolling!

Rolls are basically just tiny bread. Which means that, yes, you can technically make a pan of rolls out of any bread dough.

But first, consider the recipe and what type of rolls you're looking to make. If you want soft, fluffy pull-apart rolls (typically baked nestled together in a pan), consider starting with an enriched dough like brioche, milk bread, or challah. If you want crusty, European-style rolls (often baked on sheet trays), start with a leaner dough, such as this pain au levain.

Essentially, the type of bread you start with will determine the type of rolls you make, so plan accordingly.

Turning a bread recipe into rolls is simple: After the dough has had its first rise (otherwise known as its bulk ferment), divide it into small pieces, shape them into rolls, give them a final rise, and bake. The good news is that you don’t need to make any changes to the recipe itself — simply prepare the dough as written and leave it to undergo its first rise.

Once the bread dough has risen, it's time to divide it. Consider: How many rolls do you want, and how large do you want them to be?

Your best bet for even-sized rolls is to grab a calculator and kitchen scale. While you could divide your dough by eye, it’s faster, easier, and more accurate to use the weight measurements, if possible.

For size reference, the pre-bake weight of dinner rolls typically falls between 60g to 80g each. Imagine a 60g roll as the size of a plum when baked, while a baked 80g roll is closer to a Granny Smith apple. Moving up in the ranks are burger buns, which weigh around 100g or so pre-bake.

Here's how much each rolls should weigh before baking:

If you want small-to-medium dinner rolls: 60g to 70g

If you want medium-to-large dinner rolls: 80g to 90g

If you want extra-large dinner rolls or burger buns: 100g to 110g

Let’s say you’re using our Back-of-the-Bag Oatmeal Bread recipe. The total weight of the dough is about 830g. If your first thought is, “I want eight rolls!” you’re going to wind up with eight oat-y burger bun-sized rolls, because 830g divided by eight is just over 100g per roll. That's likely too large if you're looking to make standard dinner rolls.

To ensure you get properly sized rolls, it’s easiest to start by dividing the total weight of the dough by the weight of the size you want your rolls to be, rather than the number of rolls you want. In this case, 830g ÷ 75g = 11 large dinner rolls.

Once divided, it's time to shape the pieces of bread dough. If you’ve never shaped dinner rolls, have no fear! We have you covered, no matter the shape you choose. Basic round rolls? Got it. Fancy shapes? Yep. Braided rolls? You bet. And so much more. Often it helps to see the process in action, especially when it comes to hand positioning when shaping rolls.

For gluten-free breads, scoop the “dough” into a greased muffin pan rather than attempt to shape rolls by hand, since the dough is more like batter. If you're making medium or large gluten-free rolls, check out our Gluten-Free Dinner Rolls recipe for more details.

Small rolls won’t take as long to bake as a loaf would. Most will take around 20 to 30 minutes to bake, depending on their size. You can usually stick with the temperature your original recipe calls for, but 350°F is a safe bet, too.

A final note: Rolls baked close together in "pull-apart" style will usually take a bit longer to bake than they would if they were spaced out on a baking sheet.

And remember, if you make more rolls than you can eat in one sitting, you can always freeze and bake them.

We're diving deep on rolls ahead of Thanksgiving in our latest podcast episode, all about rolls.

#9508. The Vitamin Deficiency Linked To Chronic Headaches

Almost four in five people with chronic migraine have low levels of this vitamin.

Almost four in five people with chronic migraine have low levels of this vitamin.

Frequent headaches are linked to lower vitamin D levels.

People with chronic migraine have lower levels than those with occasional migraines or no headache disorder.

Lower vitamin D is also associated with greater muscle tenderness.

The vitamin helps muscles and nerves function, making it relevant to understanding pain.

One possibility is that low levels amplify sensitivity to pain, although this remains an explanation to investigate.

The research compared around 150 adults, divided equally between chronic migraine, episodic migraine and a group without headache disorders.

Blood tests showed low vitamin D in 78 percent of the chronic migraine group, compared with 60 percent of those with episodic migraine and 46 percent of the comparison group.

Average levels were lowest in chronic migraine and highest among those without headaches.

Chronic migraine means headaches on at least 15 days a month for more than three months, with migraine features on at least eight days.

These headaches can change in character, even within the same day, and can include pain resembling tension headaches.

Lower vitamin D levels were associated with more tenderness when muscles were pressed.

The researchers suggest that muscular discomfort and changes in pain processing could interact, potentially helping sustain headaches.

However, the association could also run in the opposite direction: people with migraine may spend less time outdoors because of light sensitivity or fatigue.

The findings do not establish that supplements prevent migraines.

Vitamin D’s established functions extend beyond maintaining strong bones.

It helps the body absorb calcium, supports muscle movement and allows nerves to carry messages between the brain and the body.

Deficiency can cause a condition called osteomalacia in adults, involving bone pain and muscle weakness.

The body produces vitamin D when sunlight reaches the skin, while food provides another source.

Oily fish, including salmon and mackerel, are among the best natural sources, while egg yolks contain smaller amounts.

Some breakfast cereals and other foods are fortified with the vitamin.

People who rarely expose their skin to sunlight can have more difficulty obtaining enough.

A blood test measures vitamin D status, helping distinguish a nutritional shortage from symptoms with other possible explanations.

The study was published in the journal Cephalalgia Reports (Prakash et al., 2026).

#9507. Forget Lemon Juice: The Spice That Brings Bright, Tangy Flavor

Elevating a meal from good to downright delicious all starts with thoughtful seasoning, each of which has a purpose; Bobby Flay says that salt and pepper lay the foundations, others bring a deep and comforting earthiness while some brighten and lift a dish entirely. Falling into the latter category is lemon juice, with just a small squeeze being all you need to bring the hidden flavors of your dish to life. But this citrus fruit isn't the only way to brighten a dish. One seriously underrated spice that's been adding lemony tartness to food for roughly 2,000 years is sumac.

Sumac is a spice beloved around the world that's criminally underused in many Western kitchens. It's important to note that we're discussing sumac as a seasoning, so we'll be focusing on the Mediterranean-slash-Levantine species rather than the North American variety (aka staghorn or smooth sumac). Before it's ground into a powder, sumac starts out as clusters of small, berry-like fruits (technically drupes) that grow on shrubs and small trees in the genus Rhus. While sumac is most commonly associated with Levantine cuisine, species of Rhus grow naturally across the Mediterranean, Africa, Asia, and even North America, so it has managed to work its way into countless cuisines. Its uses are incredibly varied, and over several millennia, everyone from the ancient Romans to Native Americans has put it to work.

To create the familiar reddish-purple ground spice, the berries are picked, left to dry in the sun, and then either stone-ground or machine-ground into a coarse powder. Sumac is most notable for its tangy, citrus-like flavor, which adds a pronounced layer of tartness to dishes. But sumac operates differently from lemon juice; its sourness is derived from malic acid, which is generally considered softer and fruitier than the sharper, more astringent citric acid found in lemon juice, making sumac an excellent substitute if you want to add a subtle brightness without putting it at the forefront.

One of our favorite things about sumac is its versatility; it can be used on everything from meat to salads and can even work in desserts. If you find yourself with a fresh batch but short on inspiration, there's no better place to look than the Levant. In Palestinian and Jordanian cooking, it's central to musakhan, a showstopping dish of roasted chicken served over taboon bread with sweet caramelized onions, olive oil, and toasted pine nuts. It's not just used in meat, either. Sumac is an essential ingredient in fattoush, a Lebanese bread and herb salad famous for its sumac-derived tang that makes it irresistibly refreshing on a hot day. Similarly, you can dust it onto Israeli salad for a refreshingly tart bite. In Syria, you can sprinkle it over your hummus or use it to take some of the sting out of fresh onion.

These are just a few of the many ways sumac is traditionally used in everyday cooking, but there are also plenty of unconventional ways to get this spice to work. Take some inspiration from the icon Alton Brown, who pairs sumac with deep-fried food. It might sound like an odd match, but sumac's bright tartness lifts the greasiness to make each bite enjoyable rather than leaving you feeling overwhelmed or oily.

Another, perhaps even more unusual, way to use sumac is as a cocktail ingredient. You could mix it with salt and use it to rim a spicy margarita for dramatic flair, or go a step further and stir some into homemade simple syrup, then strain it to create a rosy-red syrup with a tangy kick that would work wonders in fruity cocktails or, for those of our teetotal readers, mixed with lemonade or seltzer.

#9505. The two-second step to caramelize your pie crust : Just add sugar.

Most pie recipes will instruct you to sprinkle sparkling sugar or turbinado sugar on top of your egg-washed pie crust just before baking, so the coarse sugar can make those edges extra-crunchy and add a bit of glittery sheen. But why stop there — what if the bottom crust got the same treatment too?

That's what our Test Kitchen wondered while developing a new galette recipe for our newest cookbook (coming out next year!). While working on an apricot galette recipe, they tried adding a finishing sugar to the bottom of the dough before baking, and found that it created a crunchy, sugary, caramelized crust that elevated the entire dessert.

As an added bonus, this technique can help ensure a crunchy, well-browned bottom crust;  consider this step another line of defense against a soggy bottom, like baking your pie on a pizza stone or steel or baking pie on the bottom rack of the oven,

You can apply it to any pie (or galette!) recipe while rolling out the dough. Here’s how to do it:

On a lightly floured surface, roll the dough to a 10" to 12" round (aim for the smaller diameter for pie crusts, and larger for galettes). Sprinkle around 1 tablespoon of sparkling sugar or turbinado sugar all over the dough. (It’s important to only use these larger, coarse-grained sugars — we don’t recommend using granulated sugar.) Sprinkle lightly with flour, then continue to roll the dough to reach a 12" to 14" round. Carefully invert the dough round so that the sugared side is on the bottom of the pie pan (to make a single or double crust pie) or parchment paper (to make a galette).

Use this step in classic applications like apple pie where sparkling sugar can cover the entire thing, from top to bottom crust. Or, use it in custard pies like pecan or pumpkin. If you’re going the galette route for Thanksgiving, use it in our Apple Butter Apple Galette or Tiny Apple Tarts for Two. Regardless of the pie you choose, the crust — not the filling! — may be what steals the show.

#9504. Upgrade Your Next Quarter Pounder With A Request McDonald's Workers Love

The Big Mac might be McDonald's most popular burger, but there's a strong case that the Quarter Pounder is even better — we even ranked the Double Quarter Pounder with Cheese best in our McDonald's burger taste ranking. It's the only burger at McDonald's that's made to order with fresh, never-frozen beef. Alongside that tasty, fresh patty, it comes with pickles, ketchup, mustard, and freshly slivered onions. It's already in a league of its own, but McDonald's crew members have revealed you can upgrade it with a simple request that they love to use themselves.

We got the scoop from Tristen Epps-Long, winner of Season 22 of "Top Chef" and former McDonald's chef, who shared that back when he was working the line he'd "added a McChicken on with a Quarter Pounder at the same time." For those unfamiliar, the McChicken is a simple yet satisfying sandwich featuring a crispy breaded chicken patty, shredded lettuce, and creamy mayo on a regular bun. To the uninitiated, this combo might sound strange, but it's proved particularly popular online. Beyond being delicious, this pairing also happens to be great for the protein maxxers since a Quarter Pounder with Cheese already packs 30 grams of protein while the McChicken contains 14 grams, 9 of which come from the chicken patty itself, giving you almost 40 grams in one go.

Epps-Long didn't get into the specifics of how he paired the two, but there are plenty of online examples to draw inspiration from. Some order a Double Quarter Pounder (some even do the Triple) and layer an entire McChicken, bun and all, between the patties (which will give you 44 grams of protein total). If you want to cut down on the carbs, you can also request the McChicken without the bun and tuck just the crispy chicken patty, lettuce, and mayo in with the beef.

If you took a trip to the Golden Arches a decade ago, you might remember that McDonald's Quarter Pounders came with the option of adding grilled onion. Today, the only place you'll find grilled onions on the menu is the Steak, Egg, and Cheese Bagel, which disappears when the lunch menu rolls around and the Quarter Pounder makes its return. However, it seems grilled onions aren't off the table for employees. "We just grill them ourselves when we make our food," one self-identified employee claimed on Reddit.

As for customers, if you fancy swapping your regular sliced onions for grilled ones, there's no harm in asking the crew. But we warned: This little menu hack doesn't come with a 100% success rate. Some employees say it's a big no-no at their stores, but one self-identified crew member on that same Reddit thread revealed that "if you ask [nicely] we can put grilled onions on whatever you like." So it's always worth giving it a go — the worst they can say is no.

If you're obsessed with the flavor of a Big Mac, but find yourself underwhelmed by its frozen, batch-cooked patties, you're not alone. Plenty of fans have long wished for a higher-quality take on McDonald's flagship burger. While the chain has yet to make a cooked-to-order Big Mac an official menu item, fans have discovered a workaround. Simply ask the crew to add Big Mac sauce to a Double Quarter Pounder. Not only do you get those familiar tangy, creamy flavors frequently compared to Thousand Island dressing, but you also get a heartier pair of beef patties and fresh slivered onions in place of the diced, dehydrated ones used in a Big Mac.

#9503. The Overlooked Ways Love Shows Up in Urban Spaces

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

Over the past two decades, my doctoral students and I have focused on studying love, care, kindness, and compassion in urban settings. Why? Because social science research on life in America’s cities is desperately incomplete. Much like the vision of urban life that permeates most of American popular culture, social science research imagines urban areas as sites of overwhelmedness, disengagement, social and moral crisis, threat, and violence.

But, as someone who has lived and worked in large urban centers—New York City, Chicago, Detroit, Istanbul—I know firsthand that urban centers are also sites of human virtue. People in urban contexts, including those living in high-stress, oversurveilled, underresourced communities, draw daily from deep wells of love, compassion, empathy, kindness, and generosity in the service of caring for each other. From holding doors open for one another, to offering seats on buses and trains, to stopping to help with directions, to paying unexpected compliments, city-dwellers create environments that are saturated with powerful but easily missed acts of care.

My former students and I have been eager to understand how love, generosity, and care manifest and operate in the hyperdiverse, densely populated, loud, fast-paced complexities of urban spaces. Through surveys and interviews, we have sought to understand how adults residing in big cities define love, how they see love being expressed, and their views of the cascading effects of giving and receiving care, generosity, and love.

We have learned that the decision to express love and care for others in large cities is not simply a moral or emotional decision. We offer two examples of the lens needed to notice the presence of love in cities.

First, we have learned that identities matter in experiences of compassion, love, and care between strangers. Urban dwellers’ identity (for example, race or gender), lived experience, context, familial, cultural, and legal systems’ realities work together to shape decisions about whether to extend acts of love to people you do not know. For example, Kehinde, a 26-year-old African American man living in a large, densely populated city, described his experience of giving and receiving kindness, care, and love in his city as shaped by how he navigates other people seeing him as a Black man.

“I will see folks all the time that may need a hand with their bags or crossing the street or just little things like that. And I take a second, hesitate,” Kehinde says. “I don’t want to scare them. I don’t want to come off as a threat.”

To get through these moments, Kehinde describes engaging in a practice of analysis and shape-shifting. Before he steps in to offer help, he assesses the environment and changes the way he carries himself so that people will perceive him as a possible helper rather than as a threat. He says: “I smile a lot more. My voice might change a bit.” He might shrink his body and keep his head down, to avoid seeming intimidating. After helping someone, he moves along without lingering. Reflecting, he acknowledges not being his full, true self in these interactions. “I have to realize I’ve been socialized—made to believe that this is what I need to do in order to navigate the situation.” Kehinde’s story highlights the point that identities matter in economies of care. The images and stereotypes that we construct about people come at a cost even in moments of compassion. Stereotypes affect who we perceive as deserving of care, concern, and protection. Stereotypes also inform our expectations about who can be trusted to help. Stereotyping is not unique to urban settings. But because urban settings tend to be especially diverse spaces, they create abundant opportunities to study how identities and the social scripts we hold affect the way that strangers care for each other across lines of difference. What Kehinde and others bring to the fore is the reality that the targets of stereotyping are aware of the ways that they are perceived. They learn that to be seen as helpful rather than as threatening, they need to read situations correctly, make adjustments to their approaches (e.g., keep “appropriate” distance), and exit situations strategically. Targets of stereotyping must strike a balance between their own deep-seated motivations to behave caringly and their desire to stay safe. For individuals like Kehinde, miscalculations can be costly. If, in the effort to behave lovingly and compassionately, someone is misidentified as a threat, that can lead to a range of consequences from being rebuffed and embarrassed to becoming the target of violence, arrest, or death. The end result is that people consciously or unconsciously learn the rules of engagement around helping strangers.

This piece is part of a three-year GGSC project to explore love's role in promoting social well-being, bridging divides, and contributing to a good, meaningful life.

A second lesson that has emerged from studying love in urban settings is that love lives in the built environment of cities. I highlight this lesson in my Positive Psychology in Urban Settings classes. Cities are often saturated with murals, billboards, and symbols that convey messages of love, solidarity, and belonging. As residents move through neighborhood streets, they may encounter signs prominently posted in shop windows or near the entrances of religious institutions that remind them that “Black Lives Matter,” “Love Is Love,” or “Immigrants Are Welcome Here.” People display rainbow flags and national flags from apartment windows, on cars, and in other spaces, declaring both their own identities and pride for and solidarity with those identities. The architecture of urban spaces may also play a role in expressions of love and care. In many urban neighborhoods, porches, stoops, and front steps serve as places of connection and care. Simple greetings (e.g., “Morning, baby!,” “You doing good?”) voiced by neighbors sitting on their steps serve as ways of spatializing love, care, and connection in urban landscapes.

I return here to my initial point. Our studies of urban areas are desperately incomplete and will remain incomplete until we more fully examine how various forms of human goodness—including love and care—flourish in urban settings. Likewise, our understandings of love and care will remain underdeveloped until we explore how these experiences emerge in the most densely populated, diverse, complex social structures in which people live. We will truly understand love when we understand how it is titrated through place, context, history, culture, religion, structures of power, identities, and a host of individual and relational factors. Urban centers give us powerful opportunities to know love.

Jacqueline Mattis, Ph.D., is dean of the School of Arts and Sciences at Rutgers University-Newark. She studies human goodness in urban contexts.

By focusing on culture, family, and community, Jasmin Brooks Stephens says we can support mental health in Black youth long before crises occur.

In three years, I lost five loved ones, my dog, my childhood home, and my sense of invincibility. What I gained was a deeper capacity for gratitude.

Couples who embrace their own “microculture”—pet names, inside jokes, and rituals—may be happier and more satisfied with their relationship.

#9499. Ditch Plain Mayo: Spread This Flavorful Ingredient On Bread For Crispy Grilled Cheese

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Grilled cheese is a simple sandwich at its core; it can technically be made with just bread and cheese and nothing else. Of course, when something is so basic, that opens the door to a great deal of embellishment and creativity. For example, some people use butter in their pan to toast the bread and get it nice and crusty, while others, including the sandwich magicians at Disneyland, spread mayo on the outside of the sandwich to achieve a crispier texture. If that latter step appeals to you, but it just feels like something is missing, try some  mayo-adjacent garlic aioli instead.

While mayonnaise is made from egg yolks and oil, traditional aioli is an emulsion of olive oil and garlic. However, many commercial aiolis are actually just garlic-flavored mayo, with egg yolks used as a binder. Whatever the case, and however it's marketed, garlic aioli is an even more tasty spread that achieves the same crispy results as mayo, thanks to its oil content, with the addition of all the savory, slightly nutty pungency that garlic brings to the table. The spread is a simple way to add more depth of flavor to your sandwich without compromising on that craveable texture.

If you're wondering where you can find garlic aioli, good news — it's available at most major grocery stores or supermarkets, typically in the condiment aisle. You can even find it on Amazon. But if you want more control over the ingredients and flavor, you might consider making your own version at home. Even if you're a bit short on time, there's also a shortcut worth trying. You can transform store-bought mayo into aioli with just two ingredients (minced garlic and lemon juice), plus a little kosher salt.

Whatever the provenance of your garlicky spread, it couldn't be easier to use. Simply apply a layer to the outside of two slices of bread, and place them aioli-side down in a warm pan. If you're a die-hard fan of crispiness, as well as a garlic lover who can't get enough, you might actually spread the aioli on both sides of each slice of bread. Toast one side of each slice, flip, and then add your cheese (and whatever else you might want to include) and cook as usual.

Of course, garlic complements a wide range of savory flavors, so if you wanted to include bacon, play around with different cheeses beyond just American or cheddar, or top your cheese with a scoop of chili, the aioli would complement all of these options. You could even roast the garlic before adding it to your aioli for a sweeter, mellower flavor that adds another layer of depth to your grilled cheese.

#9496. The Simple Drink Swap Linked To 41% More Weight Loss

Women who changed their usual lunchtime drink lost 41 per cent more weight over 18 months. What made the difference?

Women who changed their usual lunchtime drink lost 41 per cent more weight over 18 months. What made the difference?

Swapping diet drinks for water could help people lose more weight.

Women with type 2 diabetes who make the switch lose around 41 percent more weight over 18 months than those who continue drinking diet beverages.

They are also twice as likely to achieve diabetes remission during a structured weight-management programme.

The findings raise a question about whether a drink’s calorie count tells the whole story about its effects on weight.

Sweet taste without the accompanying energy might influence appetite signals.

The results suggest that everyday drink choices could play a useful supporting role in longer-term weight management.

The research involved around 80 women who were overweight or had obesity, had type 2 diabetes and regularly consumed diet drinks.

Researchers randomly assigned them either to replace their usual diet beverage with water after lunch five times a week or to continue drinking it.

Both groups took part in a six-month weight-loss programme followed by a year devoted to maintaining their progress.

By the end, women assigned to water had lost an average of 6.82 kg, compared with 4.85 kg among those continuing with diet drinks.

The difference amounted to almost 2 kg of additional weight loss across the programme.

The water group also showed greater improvements in measures including fasting blood glucose, insulin resistance and blood fats.

Diabetes remission was reported in 90 percent of women assigned to water, compared with 45 percent of those continuing diet beverages.

Dr Hamid R. Farshchi, study co-author, said:

“It’s a small change with the potential for a big impact on long-term health outcomes.”

The brain may respond differently when a sweet taste arrives without the energy normally supplied by sugar.

In a separate experiment involving around 75 adults, participants reported greater hunger after consuming sucralose than sugar, and the sweetener altered activity in the hypothalamus, a brain region involved in appetite regulation (Chakravartti et al., 2025).

However, hunger ratings after sucralose did not differ from those after water, so the findings do not establish that sweetened drinks necessarily make people hungrier than plain water.

The mismatch between sweetness and energy might help explain some appetite responses, but whether it contributed to the weight-loss difference remains unknown.

The study was published in the journal Diabetes (Farshchi Nasr et al., 2025).

My dad put his personal pumpkin pie upstairs in the closet. About a month later, I hear a screech and come running: My mom found the pie … which was now all moldy. #9492. Can Artificial Intelligence Predict the Right Partner for You?

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

Finding love is big business (a multi-billion–dollar industry), and artificial intelligence is transforming that business. Dating apps are increasingly outsourcing user matching to AI. Recent examples range from Overtone, an AI-powered matchmaking service started by the former chief executive officer of Hinge, to SciMatch, a dating app that aims to use AI to detect compatibility from a single selfie. But can AI actually help people find love?

The promise of AI is to go deeper and end the days of endless swiping and unreturned messages. Now people can talk to AI about their hopes, dreams, and ideal partner preferences and AI can scan the pool of dating app users to find candidates who fit those criteria exactly. AI can also track behavior in the app to learn what people really want (something behavioral scientists call revealed preferences).

As a relationship scientist, I see both peril and promise in this new generation of dating apps. Despite long-heralded promises by dating app companies that their apps are based on relationship science, the truth is that there is no strong foundation of science upon which to build these matching algorithms—relationship scientists do not know what makes two particular people compatible with each other. Not yet, anyway. Sure, we know some of the factors that generally predict liking—physical attractiveness, positive personality traits, similarity, familiarity, reciprocity—but we have yet to predict with the kind of certainty dating apps might like to claim whether any two people will hit it off before they even meet.

So if a robust science of compatibility doesn’t exist yet, what is the AI matching based on? One of the first AI dating apps, Fate, uses “similarity and reciprocity of personality,” according to an interview with the founder. That sounds reasonable, and research from Amanda Montoya and her colleagues looking across 313 different studies of similarity and attraction does suggest that similarity may predict attraction—before people meet. Once people experience even a brief interaction, similarity has much less, if anything, to do with how much two people like and are attracted to each other, as seen in an analysis of actual and perceived similarity of personality traits in potential partners, by Sarah Humberg and her colleagues. A systematic inquiry from my research lab, led by Annika From, also yielded little evidence that romantic couples are happier if partners are more similar to each other.

What about “reciprocity of personality”? If this phrase refers to the idea that two people may have complementary personalities that meld well together, this theory of compatibility, unfortunately, has even less empirical support.

Perhaps it is not too concerning that we lack a strong, agreed-upon scientific basis for predicting compatibility. After all, one of the great promises of AI is that it will learn as it goes, based not just on what a user says they want, but how they actually behave (who they swipe right on, whom they actually chat with after matching). Emerging evidence from different fields suggests that AI may be able to detect complex patterns that humans have been unable to discern. In the medical field, AI has been used to create more precise and accurate predictions that are aiding diagnosis and treatment. From weather prediction to fraud detection, the use of AI has enhanced forecasting. So maybe it can do the same for our love lives?

If the problem has simply been that we have not been able to identify the complex patterns that make up human compatibility, then AI may, in fact, be the answer. If, however, the problem is that humans themselves are too complex, then AI may not get us any closer to being able to forecast love.

What do I mean by this? Well, researchers have found that people will list their preferred partner traits before taking part in a speed dating event, only to have all those preferences go out the window when they actually interact with people. In my own work, I have discovered that people will dismiss another user’s dating app profile for reasons like “same name as my brother” and “bad haircut.” Yes, they will rule someone out as the possible love of their life because of something as irrelevant as their name (give them a nickname!) or hairstyle (arguably our most changeable physical characteristic).

Why do I bring up these examples? They raise the question of whether AI even has the right information to rely on when gathering data based on people’s stated preferences or swiping behavior. So what data might AI need? In my lab, we hope to find some answers to this question with a series of studies that aim to combine dating-app data with real-life interactions. This project will allow us to see what chemistry looks like online and offline, uncover who has online chemistry that translates into real-world sparks, and identify the factors that make chemistry more likely between two people (if there are any meaningful predictors).

The truth is, researchers at the forefront of this work do not always agree on whether forecasting love is even possible. While many relationship scientists have devoted their careers to testing the complex ways in which personalities and preferences interact to predict compatibility, they have arrived at different conclusions. Some researchers believe it will be possible to build an algorithm to predict compatibility; these researchers would likely see the promise in AI. On the other hand, there are those who have concluded that compatibility is a dynamic process that evolves as two people interact with each other and cannot be predicted ahead of time. For these researchers, finding love is less about the perfect match and more about being in the right place at the right time and then building love together through shared moments, from special nicknames and in-jokes to regular rituals just the two of you share.

This piece is part of a three-year GGSC project to explore love's role in promoting social well-being, bridging divides, and contributing to a good, meaningful life.

With the research projects in my lab, we hope to test these theories by having people meet different numbers of times. We’ve seen from our early work that pairing two random people together does not typically produce high levels of chemistry. That instant attraction seems to be relatively rare; but what if they met repeatedly? Could chemistry develop? Does it need some sort of initial spark to set it off, and can we create that spark with the right equipment, such as a well-placed question or activity that brings two people together? In other words, is chemistry possible with anyone if the right conditions were met, or is there some, as yet undiscovered, set of requirements for two people to be able to fall in love?

I don’t know the answer to these questions yet, nor does the field of relationship science, although many have theories. I see AI as both an exciting tool that might help us answer this question as well as a technology that people looking for love should employ with caution. When used as a way to explore and test models of compatibility, AI may yield invaluable insights. But we must always remember that AI is trained with specific beliefs about what makes two people compatible. If researchers do not yet know what makes two people compatible, then letting AI do all the work to vet potential partners means you are only going to see the people that AI thinks are right for you, while likely remaining in the dark about how AI decided they’re a good match. This gap in knowledge may keep you from meeting someone unexpectedly compatible with you.

An alternative approach to dating is to think about it as a time for exploration. Instead of only connecting with people who have similar facial structures or reciprocal personalities, try dating people with all kinds of different experiences, personalities, beliefs, and desires. If you go this route, Paul Eastwick offers a valuable piece of advice in his recent book Bonded by Evolution: for those who have serious dealbreakers (e.g., you know you want children, have strong religious views, or do not eat meat), go ahead and surround yourself with people who share those views. This will help you avoid facing potentially difficult lifestyle tradeoffs in the future if you do find yourself falling in love. But don’t eliminate someone just because of a bad haircut or a shared name. Instead, be open to exploring and then see for yourself who you connect with and who you do not. You might end up being surprised.

Amie M. Gordon, Ph.D., is a social-personality psychologist who takes a dynamic, dyadic approach to investigating the affective, social-cognitive, and biological processes that shape interpersonal relationships. Her research has been published in top academic journals as well as featured in popular news outlets such as The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal, and The Atlantic. She received her PhD in Social-Personality Psychology from UC Berkeley and her BA in Psychology from UCLA. She blogs for Psychology Today in Between You and Me, and is currently completing a postdoctoral research fellowship at the University of California, San Francisco.

#9482. Am I Doing This Right? Teen Edition

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

Parenting a teen can sometimes make you nostalgic for the early years, when you could still scoop up a frustrated toddler and redirect her with bubbles. In the teen years, sweet hugs can provoke eye rolls; a well-intentioned “How was your day?” may be misconstrued as meddling.

That’s just your teens becoming independent. Decades of research finds that portraying adolescence as a period of “storm and stress” is not only misguided, it’s harmful. In fact, developmental science shows this time of life is better recast as “the breakthrough years.” According to research on over one thousand adolescents by Ellen Galinsky, author and president of Families and Work Institute, there are key messages that teens want to get through to adults:

None of this is easy, of course. Along the way, tough situations crop up, and it’s hard to know what to do. Here are common questions, with answers backed by scientists and their research.

Q: My 16-year-old doesn’t seem to be motivated to do anything beyond hanging out with friends and playing video games. When I bring up the prospect of college, he says he doesn’t care. What should I do?

A: As parents, we want to set our high schoolers up for success. But, at that age, young people are still trying to figure out who they are, what interests them, and what their future looks like. “Identity development and purpose formation are underway, but rarely fully formed by high school,” says Kendall Cotton Bronk, professor of psychology at Claremont Graduate University.

Not finding any answers yet is expected. “Parents need to remind themselves that where their child is at this moment in time isn’t necessarily where they will be in the future,” says Bronk.

To help teens along, encourage them to try different activities at school and in the community, whether it’s, for instance, robotics, the debate team, chorus, improv, or the school paper. Leave it to them to select what to try. Don’t do it for them. Don’t judge their choices.

“While it’s not appropriate for parents to be too directive, they can help their teenager reflect on what they liked and didn’t like and what felt meaningful and not so meaningful about their various experiences,” says Bronk. “Having someone to debrief with can help them deepen their reflection and more quickly identify a purposeful direction.”

Research suggests that when teens are guided by their own interests, free of external pressures, they’re more likely to take charge of their own career development. But when parents are overly involved in their adolescents’ lives, says Bronk, young people don’t have an opportunity to cultivate a sense of agency, and this can make career development planning a big challenge.

Instead of trying to manage their path, says Bronk, parents should simply “be curious.” Ask your child: What interests you? What feels satisfying for you?

“This kind of questioning can scaffold and deepen their young person’s reflections, and reflection is a key component of figuring out what kind of path a young person wants to follow,” she says. “Usually, what holds their interest is something they’re good at and care about, and that allows them to make a meaningful difference in the broader world,” she explains.

Taking advantage of volunteer opportunities can help young people see themselves as useful and discover careers that might interest them—for instance, helping out in a food pantry, animal shelter, a kids sports organization, or hospital. Encourage your teen to ask people he knows about their jobs, what they entail, and what they studied to get there.

Finally, don’t assume that your child’s lack of direction is apathy. Whatever their interest is, “work with it, not against it,” says Bronk. “At the same time, be patient. It may just be the case that they haven’t figured it all out yet. Their timetable may not be the same as yours, but they will eventually get there. Remember, this isn’t a race.”

Q: My 15-year-old seems to be living a separate life. He spends most of his time in his room and has dinner more often with his friends than with us. How can we encourage him to be a part of the family?

A: Seeking independence (while still navigating being dependent on adults) is one of the primary tasks of adolescents as they transition to becoming more self-sufficient into early adulthood.

“I try to get parents to understand that it’s not about them,” says Laurence Steinberg, author of You and Your Adolescent. “The parents didn’t do anything wrong; the child isn’t rejecting them. This is a sign they’re growing up normally. It’s partly wanting to make their own decisions and have their own life, but it’s also wanting emotional independence—to show that they are more than their parents’ kid.”

Chances are a closed door doesn’t mean trouble. Just as most adults don’t want others listening in on their calls, teens don’t want that either. They’re not distancing themselves from you, but simply distancing themselves from being a child.

“There’s nothing the parents can do to stop this from happening,” says Steinberg, a professor emeritus of psychology and neuroscience at Temple University. “And they shouldn’t try.”

That said, spending time with family is also important. To suggest that, say something like, “We want to spend more time with you, but we also know that spending time with friends is important. What’s the best way to catch up with you?” By making the planning of it a collaborative process, your child is more likely to stay engaged. Research suggests that they may even find the activity more enjoyable.

Only rarely is a shut bedroom door cause for concern—for instance, you notice other behavioral changes, such as a drop in grades, a dwindling interest in his usual in-person activities. If you suspect an issue, let your child know that you’re there for him, and that he can get professional help, too.

One last note: If your child is spending most of his time in his room online, setting limits on its own may not be enough, says Jacqueline Nesi, author of the Techno Sapiens newsletter and associate professor of psychiatry and human behavior at Brown University. You’ll also want to discuss with them what you want for him and what he wants.

The evidence also supports “co-viewing” or “co-using” technology with your kids, whether that’s a video game, TV, or an AI chatbot, says Nesi. Using tech together can spark conversation and help parents better understand their kids’ digital lives.

That said, it’s still important for you to protect their sleep and to make sure that they live a life in person. Again, to get their buy-in, decide on screen-time parameters, and replace screen time with in-person activities he might enjoy, such cooking a favorite meal together or an outing with family and friends.

Q: My 17-year-old daughter recently suffered a breakup. How can I help her feel better without intruding?

A: Even if a relationship doesn’t look like a monogamous romantic relationship in adulthood (it may be short, or the partners may not talk to each other very much), these breakups can still be painful. So always take your teen’s romantic activities seriously, as well as the emotions they are experiencing following a breakup, says Emily Bibby, a researcher at the Relationship Development Center at Stony Brook University. Be compassionate, validating, and nonjudgmental. Let her know that she is having a normal reaction to a difficult situation.

Allow space to grieve and vent. “Listen hard to what your child is thinking and feeling,” says Barry Farber, professor of psychology and education at Columbia University Teachers College. “Ask what they’ve learned from the relationship. Framing the relationship as a learning experience, as opposed to a failure, can help nurture resilience and personal growth, and can help her feel more in control and more hopeful about future relationships.”

As Farber and his coauthors point out in a recent study, while time doesn’t necessarily “heal all wounds” (because memories and thoughts can linger), it almost always “softens the blow” when other strategies are also employed, such as talking with a trusted friend or family member. While the study involved mostly white, female adult subjects, the same principle generally applies across ages, genders, and ethnicities. Letting your child know that things will get better can help.

Trying to convince a teen to do anything is difficult, says Farber, so it’s better to simply listen, and then only encourage as opposed to insisting or dictating. Encourage her to engage in activities she enjoys, whether it’s treating herself to an afternoon manicure, going to a concert, or spending time in nature like hiking and walking on the beach. Encourage her to avoid all contact with her ex, both in person and on social media. If one person believes it’s really over, a clean break is usually best, says Farber. Any surge of adrenaline that happens when you see your ex in any form is only temporary, and only makes it harder to get over the breakup.

If sad feelings are impairing day-to-day life—she’s not seeing friends, she’s failing her classes, there’s a dramatic change in eating or sleeping—have her consider seeking help from a mental health professional. “Therapy normalizes the experience,” says Farber. “It helps people find a new narrative when they’re stuck.”

Therapy also gives people an opportunity to share their feelings in a private space and learn evidence-based emotion-regulation skills to improve their mental health and functioning, says Bibby.

This workbook is for a range of practitioners who support parents and caregivers of children between preschool and high school.

If your teen is debilitatingly depressed or harming herself, then advise that she get professional help as soon as possible, such as from her school psychologist, her primary care doctor (for a referral), or a therapist you think highly of.

To help their teen navigate relationships in general, parents can model healthy relationships with not just a partner, but also friends and family members. Teaching your teen effective communication skills and boundary setting early on, in the context of friendships and family relationships, can prove helpful once your teen starts dating, says Bibby, who recently coauthored a research review on romantic relationships and mental health in adolescents.

And as for parents of teens who are just becoming interested in dating, it’s helpful to talk about what healthy relationships look like, emphasizing the importance of mutual respect. “Thinking through what they would do [in different dating scenarios] and how to navigate different challenges that may arise can build confidence when they start dating,” says Bibby.

Q: My 14-year-old has found herself in a friend group that spends a lot of money on expensive clothing and electronics. We don’t approve of these teens and don’t share their consumerist values. How do we prevent our child from becoming materialistic, too?

A: You can empower your teen to make thoughtful, confident choices about money, friendships, and the pressures they face. Try leading with connection rather than control: Talk openly about your family’s values, help them practice setting boundaries, and remind them they do not need to match their friends’ spending to belong or feel worthy. Expensive tastes and social media pressures can be hard to ignore, but your teen can learn to make choices that reflect what matters most to them.

People turn to materialistic things to fill a void, but that’s only a temporary fix, says Lan Nguyen Chaplin, a professor of integrated marketing communications at Northwestern University, and an expert in children’s and teens’ consumer behavior. “They end up in a vicious cycle of wanting and needing more to fill the same void because material things cannot fill real voids.”

In her research exploring materialism in a group of 12- to 18-year-olds, she reported that those with high self-esteem were less likely to have materialistic tendencies. “Parents and peers [are] a source of emotional support and psychological well-being,” she writes. “Supportive parents and peers boost adolescents’ self-esteem, which decreases their need to turn to material goods to develop positive self-perceptions.”

Read this article in Spanish on La Red Hispana, the public-facing media outlet and distribution house of HCN, focused on educating, inspiring, and informing 40 million U.S. Hispanics.

To that end, start at home and help your kids feel good about themselves. Gratitude journals can be a good way to curb materialism, but, of course, asking a teen who is new to journaling to start one can feel like a homework writing assignment if it’s yet another thing they are required to do. Rather, approach it with a light touch. Model gratitude by sharing with your teen who and what you’re grateful for, keep a gratitude journal yourself, or ask them what the high point of their day is.

It also helps to stop tying accomplishments to material things. So, instead of, say, rewarding a good report card with money or sneakers, celebrate the hard work that was put into achieving the good grades over a fun experience together like a movie night at home.

Most of all, spend time with your teen in lighthearted and playful ways, no matter how short. Even a 10-minute car ride can be a good opportunity to connect with them, and also reinforce the good things they have going for them, Chaplin says.

Joanne Chen is a writer and editor in New York City. Her articles on children and parenting have appeared in The Bump, Parents Magazine, and the New York Times.

By focusing on culture, family, and community, Jasmin Brooks Stephens says we can support mental health in Black youth long before crises occur.

A therapist explains how having kids can change our perspective on how our parents treated us, for better or worse.
